sources.title: Binance replaces 90% of stolen crypto after record $6.3 billion hack, pledges to cover remaining losses
passages: Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has replaced 90% of the assets stolen in a record $6.3 billion hack by using its own funds to purchase replacement tokens, the company said on Saturday.
The remaining 10% comprises less liquid tokens, which could take longer to acquire, Binance said in a statement posted on X.
sources.body: Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has replaced 90% of the assets stolen in a record $6.3 billion hack by using its own funds to purchase replacement tokens, the company said on Saturday. The remaining 10% comprises less liquid tokens, which could take longer to acquire, Binance said in a statement posted on X.

extraction.body: Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has replaced 90% of the assets stolen in a record $6.3 billion hack by using its own funds to purchase replacement tokens, the company said on Saturday. The remaining 10% comprises less liquid tokens, which could take longer to acquire, Binance said in a statement posted on X. "We've now replenished 90% of the stolen assets, and we're committed to covering the remaining 10%. Our users will not bear the financial impact of this incident," co-CEO Richard Teng said in a post on X on Saturday. Binance assures users of fund safety after cyberattack Cryptocurrency prices declined on Friday as Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, sought to reassure customers that their funds remained safe following the theft of more than $6 billion worth of digital assets.Analysts have blamed North Korea for the cyberattack.Teng said on Friday that the breach was a "complex attack" involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to erase evidence of its activities, making the incident more difficult to trace and investigate.Binance sets aside $6.34 billion to cover lossesFollowing the hack, Binance temporarily suspended customer withdrawals. However, the exchange said on Saturday that it remained on track to resume withdrawals on Sunday.The company added that it had internally allocated around $6.34 billion from its own funds to cover the losses.The money spent re-buying tokens came from using part of its $1 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures insurance fund, and the company's own corporate treasury, it said on X.Binance also said it had taken a new snapshot of assets held on its platform as of 0000 GMT on October 31, as part of its proof-of-reserves process.Users holding the 10 listed tokens — BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC — would be able to verify that their assets were backed at a minimum 1:1 ratio once the full proof was available, it said.

sources.title: Binance says 90% of $6.3 billion in crypto stolen in hack replenished
passages: Two days after analysts said North Korean hackers likely executed a brazen $6.3 billion crypto heist on the blockchain platform Binance, the company says it has replenished about $5.7 billion in the stolen assets.
In an update on Saturday morning, Binance said it tapped its corporate treasury to purchase billions of dollars in crypto from the market and private brokers.

"Our users will not bear the financial impact of this incident." Binance already had an emergency fund of about $1 billion for situations like this, but the unprecedented scale of the attack rendered that piggy bank insufficient to cover the losses.
In 2025, the FBI named the same group responsible for a $1.5 billion hack on Bybit, another crypto exchange.
On Thursday, around 4 p.m., Binance reported a security breach on its blockchain network that it initially said was made possible by a compromised employee laptop.
To remediate the heist, Binance also tapped into its Futures Insurance Fund, a regulatory requirement typically used to protect traders against losses suffered during extreme market conditions.

extraction.body: Two days after analysts said North Korean hackers likely executed a brazen $6.3 billion crypto heist on the blockchain platform Binance, the company says it has replenished about $5.7 billion in the stolen assets. In an update on Saturday morning, Binance said it tapped its corporate treasury to purchase billions of dollars in crypto from the market and private brokers. "We've now replenished 90% of the stolen assets, and we're committed to covering the remaining 10%," Richard Teng, the company's co-CEO, said on X. "Our users will not bear the financial impact of this incident." Binance already had an emergency fund of about $1 billion for situations like this, but the unprecedented scale of the attack rendered that piggy bank insufficient to cover the losses. To remediate the heist, Binance also tapped into its Futures Insurance Fund, a regulatory requirement typically used to protect traders against losses suffered during extreme market conditions. Binance said on Saturday that it plans to resume withdrawals on Sunday. Like a bank, Binance holds assets deposited by customers, who rely on the company to safeguard their funds and return them when requested. On Thursday, around 4 p.m., Binance reported a security breach on its blockchain network that it initially said was made possible by a compromised employee laptop. The company later revised this assessment, saying the attack was broader in scope. Some blockchain intelligence firms said the breach was likely the work of an elite North Korean hacker group called TraderTraitor, noting similarities to its previous attacks. In 2025, the FBI named the same group responsible for a $1.5 billion hack on Bybit, another crypto exchange. Within minutes, the hackers had siphoned billions of dollars in cryptocurrency from Binance-controlled wallets. According to analysts, the hackers used automated scripts to rapidly transfer the money around in an apparent attempt to launder it. Stablecoin issuers reacted quickly by freezing funds in traceable currencies, but the hackers still managed to convert about $786 million into comparably untraceable currencies, intelligence platform Elliptic said. Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence platform, told Business Insider on Friday that the North Korean hackers are likely moving to offload their pilfered funds into the country's weapons program. "When North Korea steals at this scale, the money supports weapons proliferation, and every dollar we freeze or trace is a dollar the regime loses," Redbord said in an email.

extraction.body: Binance said Saturday that it has covered up to 90% of the roughly $6.3 billion in token assets stolen from its hot wallets in a record crypto theft announced Thursday. Binance said it will continue to buy the remaining relevant token assets through market and over-the-counter channels until the covered amount reaches 100% for all tokens. "All BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC are fully backed 100%," Binance said in a statement . "Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users." The exchange said the outstanding 10% consists of tokens outside its top 10 that are "less liquid, which means they may take longer to source in the required amounts." Binance said it is tapping its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a portion of its Futures insurance fund, and its corporate treasury to replenish the assets. "Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident. We will continue to demonstrate this commitment through measurable progress, transparent reporting, and concrete actions," Binance said. Its "next milestone" will be resuming withdrawal services for users by Sunday, subject to security checks, while the exchange continues its investigation into the attack, it said. Binance declined to discuss additional details or updates on its investigation to CNBC, referring questions to its latest statement. It still isn't clear how the attack — the largest crypto theft on record — took place. The world's largest crypto exchange initially said the hack may involve "a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions." However, Co-CEO Richard Teng later said the attack involved a more complex process rather than the misuse of a single engineer's permissions. It also wasn't clear who was responsible for the breach. But TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and AI investigations company, pointed to North Korean hackers as the potential culprits . "Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack and the KelpDAO hack in April 2026: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet, staging that began well before the theft, and signatures obtained in advance then executed in one burst," the company said. — CNBC's Jenny Lee, Liz Napolitano and Davis Giangiulio contributed to this report. Binance said on Saturday that it plans to resume withdrawals on Sunday. Like a bank, Binance holds assets deposited by customers, who rely on the company to safeguard their funds and return them when requested. On Thursday, around 4 p.m., Binance reported a security breach on its blockchain network that it initially said was made possible by a compromised employee laptop. The company later revised this assessment, saying the attack was broader in scope. Some blockchain intelligence firms said the breach was likely the work of an elite North Korean hacker group called TraderTraitor, noting similarities to its previous attacks. In 2025, the FBI named the same group responsible for a $1.5 billion hack on Bybit, another crypto exchange. Within minutes, the hackers had siphoned billions of dollars in cryptocurrency from Binance-controlled wallets. According to analysts, the hackers used automated scripts to rapidly transfer the money around in an apparent attempt to launder it. Stablecoin issuers reacted quickly by freezing funds in traceable currencies, but the hackers still managed to convert about $786 million into comparably untraceable currencies, intelligence platform Elliptic said. Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence platform, told Business Insider on Friday that the North Korean hackers are likely moving to offload their pilfered funds into the country's weapons program. "When North Korea steals at this scale, the money supports weapons proliferation, and every dollar we freeze or trace is a dollar the regime loses," Redbord said in an email.

Binance has not independently confirmed the identity of those responsible.Binance's latest announcement marks a significant step in its efforts to restore customer confidence, with the resumption of withdrawals on Sunday emerging as the next major test for the exchange.You use AI every day.

sources.title: Binance says 90% of $6.3 billion hack losses are now covered, plans to resume withdrawals Sunday - CNBC
passages: Binance said Saturday that it has covered up to 90% of the roughly $6.3 billion in token assets stolen from its hot wallets in a record crypto theft announced Thursday.
Binance declined to discuss additional details or updates on its investigation to CNBC, referring questions to its latest statement.
"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident.
We will continue to demonstrate this commitment through measurable progress, transparent reporting, and concrete actions," Binance said.
Its "next milestone" will be resuming withdrawal services for users by Sunday, subject to security checks, while the exchange continues its investigation into the attack, it said.

"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack and the KelpDAO hack in April 2026: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet, staging that began well before the theft, and signatures obtained in advance then executed in one burst," the company said.
Binance said it is tapping its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a portion of its Futures insurance fund, and its corporate treasury to replenish the assets.

The world's largest crypto exchange initially said the hack may involve "a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions." However, Co-CEO Richard Teng later said the attack involved a more complex process rather than the misuse of a single engineer's permissions.
— CNBC's Jenny Lee, Liz Napolitano and Davis Giangiulio contributed to this report.

extraction.body: Binance said Saturday that it has covered up to 90% of the roughly $6.3 billion in token assets stolen from its hot wallets in a record crypto theft announced Thursday. Binance said it will continue to buy the remaining relevant token assets through market and over-the-counter channels until the covered amount reaches 100% for all tokens. "All BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC are fully backed 100%," Binance said in a statement . "Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users." The exchange said the outstanding 10% consists of tokens outside its top 10 that are "less liquid, which means they may take longer to source in the required amounts." Binance said it is tapping its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a portion of its Futures insurance fund, and its corporate treasury to replenish the assets. "Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident. We will continue to demonstrate this commitment through measurable progress, transparent reporting, and concrete actions," Binance said. Its "next milestone" will be resuming withdrawal services for users by Sunday, subject to security checks, while the exchange continues its investigation into the attack, it said. Binance declined to discuss additional details or updates on its investigation to CNBC, referring questions to its latest statement. It still isn't clear how the attack — the largest crypto theft on record — took place. The world's largest crypto exchange initially said the hack may involve "a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions." However, Co-CEO Richard Teng later said the attack involved a more complex process rather than the misuse of a single engineer's permissions. It also wasn't clear who was responsible for the breach. But TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and AI investigations company, pointed to North Korean hackers as the potential culprits . "Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack and the KelpDAO hack in April 2026: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet, staging that began well before the theft, and signatures obtained in advance then executed in one burst," the company said. — CNBC's Jenny Lee, Liz Napolitano and Davis Giangiulio contributed to this report. sources.title: Binance replaces 90% of stolen crypto after record $6.3 billion hack, pledges to cover remaining losses
passages: Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has replaced 90% of the assets stolen in a record $6.3 billion hack by using its own funds to purchase replacement tokens, the company said on Saturday.
The remaining 10% comprises less liquid tokens, which could take longer to acquire, Binance said in a statement posted on X.

The remaining 10% comprises less liquid tokens, which could take longer to acquire, Binance said in a statement posted on X.

extraction.body: Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has replaced 90% of the assets stolen in a record $6.3 billion hack by using its own funds to purchase replacement tokens, the company said on Saturday. The remaining 10% comprises less liquid tokens, which could take longer to acquire, Binance said in a statement posted on X. "We've now replenished 90% of the stolen assets, and we're committed to covering the remaining 10%. Our users will not bear the financial impact of this incident," co-CEO Richard Teng said in a post on X on Saturday. Binance assures users of fund safety after cyberattack Cryptocurrency prices declined on Friday as Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, sought to reassure customers that their funds remained safe following the theft of more than $6 billion worth of digital assets.Analysts have blamed North Korea for the cyberattack.Teng said on Friday that the breach was a "complex attack" involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to erase evidence of its activities, making the incident more difficult to trace and investigate.Binance sets aside $6.34 billion to cover lossesFollowing the hack, Binance temporarily suspended customer withdrawals. However, the exchange said on Saturday that it remained on track to resume withdrawals on Sunday.The company added that it had internally allocated around $6.34 billion from its own funds to cover the losses.The money spent re-buying tokens came from using part of its $1 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures insurance fund, and the company's own corporate treasury, it said on X.Binance also said it had taken a new snapshot of assets held on its platform as of 0000 GMT on October 31, as part of its proof-of-reserves process.Users holding the 10 listed tokens — BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC — would be able to verify that their assets were backed at a minimum 1:1 ratio once the full proof was available, it said.

sources.title: Binance says 90% of $6.3 billion in crypto stolen in hack replenished
passages: Two days after analysts said North Korean hackers likely executed a brazen $6.3 billion crypto heist on the blockchain platform Binance, the company says it has replenished about $5.7 billion in the stolen assets.
In an update on Saturday morning, Binance said it tapped its corporate treasury to purchase billions of dollars in crypto from the market and private brokers.

"Our users will not bear the financial impact of this incident." Binance already had an emergency fund of about $1 billion for situations like this, but the unprecedented scale of the attack rendered that piggy bank insufficient to cover the losses.
In 2025, the FBI named the same group responsible for a $1.5 billion hack on Bybit, another crypto exchange.
On Thursday, around 4 p.m., Binance reported a security breach on its blockchain network that it initially said was made possible by a compromised employee laptop.
To remediate the heist, Binance also tapped into its Futures Insurance Fund, a regulatory requirement typically used to protect traders against losses suffered during extreme market conditions.

extraction.body: Two days after analysts said North Korean hackers likely executed a brazen $6.3 billion crypto heist on the blockchain platform Binance, the company says it has replenished about $5.7 billion in the stolen assets. In an update on Saturday morning, Binance said it tapped its corporate treasury to purchase billions of dollars in crypto from the market and private brokers. "We've now replenished 90% of the stolen assets, and we're committed to covering the remaining 10%," Richard Teng, the company's co-CEO, said on X. "Our users will not bear the financial impact of this incident." Binance already had an emergency fund of about $1 billion for situations like this, but the unprecedented scale of the attack rendered that piggy bank insufficient to cover the losses. To remediate the heist, Binance also tapped into its Futures Insurance Fund, a regulatory requirement typically used to protect traders against losses suffered during extreme market conditions. Binance said on Saturday that it plans to resume withdrawals on Sunday. Like a bank, Binance holds assets deposited by customers, who rely on the company to safeguard their funds and return them when requested. On Thursday, around 4 p.m., Binance reported a security breach on its blockchain network that it initially said was made possible by a compromised employee laptop. The company later revised this assessment, saying the attack was broader in scope. Some blockchain intelligence firms said the breach was likely the work of an elite North Korean hacker group called TraderTraitor, noting similarities to its previous attacks. In 2025, the FBI named the same group responsible for a $1.5 billion hack on Bybit, another crypto exchange. Within minutes, the hackers had siphoned billions of dollars in cryptocurrency from Binance-controlled wallets. According to analysts, the hackers used automated scripts to rapidly transfer the money around in an apparent attempt to launder it. Stablecoin issuers reacted quickly by freezing funds in traceable currencies, but the hackers still managed to convert about $786 million into comparably untraceable currencies, intelligence platform Elliptic said. Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence platform, told Business Insider on Friday that the North Korean hackers are likely moving to offload their pilfered funds into the country's weapons program. "When North Korea steals at this scale, the money supports weapons proliferation, and every dollar we freeze or trace is a dollar the regime loses," Redbord said in an email.

extraction.body: Binance said Saturday that it has covered up to 90% of the roughly $6.3 billion in token assets stolen from its hot wallets in a record crypto theft announced Thursday. Binance said it will continue to buy the remaining relevant token assets through market and over-the-counter channels until the covered amount reaches 100% for all tokens. "All BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC are fully backed 100%," Binance said in a statement . "Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users." The exchange said the outstanding 10% consists of tokens outside its top 10 that are "less liquid, which means they may take longer to source in the required amounts." Binance said it is tapping its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a portion of its Futures insurance fund, and its corporate treasury to replenish the assets. "Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident. We will continue to demonstrate this commitment through measurable progress, transparent reporting, and concrete actions," Binance said. Its "next milestone" will be resuming withdrawal services for users by Sunday, subject to security checks, while the exchange continues its investigation into the attack, it said. Binance declined to discuss additional details or updates on its investigation to CNBC, referring questions to its latest statement. It still isn't clear how the attack — the largest crypto theft on record — took place. The world's largest crypto exchange initially said the hack may involve "a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions." However, Co-CEO Richard Teng later said the attack involved a more complex process rather than the misuse of a single engineer's permissions. It also wasn't clear who was responsible for the breach. But TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and AI investigations company, pointed to North Korean hackers as the potential culprits . "Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack and the KelpDAO hack in April 2026: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet, staging that began well before the theft, and signatures obtained in advance then executed in one burst," the company said. — CNBC's Jenny Lee, Liz Napolitano and Davis Giangiulio contributed to this report. To remediate the heist, Binance also tapped into its Futures Insurance Fund, a regulatory requirement typically used to protect traders against losses suffered during extreme market conditions. Binance said on Saturday that it plans to resume withdrawals on Sunday. Like a bank, Binance holds assets deposited by customers, who rely on the company to safeguard their funds and return them when requested. On Thursday, around 4 p.m., Binance reported a security breach on its blockchain network that it initially said was made possible by a compromised employee laptop. The company later revised this assessment, saying the attack was broader in scope. Some blockchain intelligence firms said the breach was likely the work of an elite North Korean hacker group called TraderTraitor, noting similarities to its previous attacks. In 2025, the FBI named the same group responsible for a $1.5 billion hack on Bybit, another crypto exchange. Within minutes, the hackers had siphoned billions of dollars in cryptocurrency from Binance-controlled wallets. According to analysts, the hackers used automated scripts to rapidly transfer the money around in an apparent attempt to launder it. Stablecoin issuers reacted quickly by freezing funds in traceable currencies, but the hackers still managed to convert about $786 million into comparably untraceable currencies, intelligence platform Elliptic said. Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence platform, told Business Insider on Friday that the North Korean hackers are likely moving to offload their pilfered funds into the country's weapons program. "When North Korea steals at this scale, the money supports weapons proliferation, and every dollar we freeze or trace is a dollar the regime loses," Redbord said in an email.

sources.title: Cracks are emerging in the AI spending boom

extraction.body: Investors are getting nervous about AI infrastructure spending just as the Big Tech companies double down. Over the past two weeks, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft have outlined plans to spend more than $740 billion on capital expenditures this year, which Wall Street is reading as AI infrastructure spending, including data centers and chips. Earlier in the AI boom, investors largely rewarded such big outlays, viewing them as a sign of confidence in the technology’s growth potential. But as we enter the fourth quarter, that enthusiasm seems to be giving way to concerns about negative free cash flow (spending more cash than a company brings in), mounting debt, and whether these enormous investments will ever generate enough returns. The anxiety spilled across the market on Friday. The Nasdaq fell 2.9%, and chip stocks took a drubbing, too: Nvidia dropped 4%, Broadcom more than 5%, and Qualcomm 11%. Alphabet, which plummeted 12% on Thursday, its worst day on record, wiping out $500 billion in market value, fell again. A big part of the concern is that companies that used to have overflowing free cash flow from their core businesses are getting hit as AI threatens the economics of those businesses. Alphabet provided the clearest example of that this week. Google’s parent company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the third quarter, its second consecutive quarter in the red, even as quarterly capex grew to $51.4 billion. Alphabet expects to spend up to $205 billion this year, and expects that spending to keep rising in 2027. Meanwhile, the wild success of AI Mode — Google’s AI-powered chatbot feature built directly into Search — is eating into the company’s money-maker. Google’s Search advertising business, which makes up roughly half of its revenue, saw growth slow to 12%, its weakest pace in five quarters. That leaves Google walking a tightrope. It’s spending billions on the AI technology that could undermine the search business that pays it. Amazon is in a similar boat after reporting negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with $14.8 billion in positive free cash flow the year before. The company says it expects to spend $220 billion in capex this year. Even though revenue at its cloud business, AWS, grew 39%, Amazon’s stock tumbled 7% after it reported earnings Thursday. Meta is also burning cash, reporting negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in the third quarter as capex outpaced its operating cash. It’s guiding to as much as $145 billion in capex this year. The company noted that Muse, its new free personal AI agent, is a bit of a money pit (it’s “very compute-intensive to run,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said). But ad revenue grew 26%. Still, no amount of good news saved Meta from taking a 10% hit on its stock last week. Microsoft was the only exception when it came to free cash flow — it recorded $18.6 billion in positive free cash flow in its latest quarter, with spending on capex at $45.2 billion, less than the $50 billion it projected. Microsoft said that wasn’t an intentional pullback from AI spending, blaming delays in capacity from third-party providers. As a result, shares of smaller companies that rent out AI computing power sank . It’s worth noting that the money to pay for all of this AI infrastructure isn’t just coming from the Big Tech companies’ profits. It’s also showing up in stock and bond sales. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle raised a combined $326 billion in debt in 2026, triple the amount raised last year. Demand for AI compute remains strong. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft all saw gains in their cloud businesses. But investors are getting spooked by the costs of meeting that demand. These muddied waters could complicate Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO. The AI company filed to go public earlier this week, and its future growth depends on securing enormous amounts of compute. Financial Times reported Friday that Blackstone has warned investors the company might not qualify for an investment-grade rating after its IPO, meaning it might end up being more reliant on the hyperscalers and third-parties to fund its infrastructure ambitions. Rebecca Bellan is a senior reporter at TechCrunch where she covers the business, policy, and emerging trends shaping artificial intelligence. Her work has also appeared in Forbes, Bloomberg, The Atlantic, The Daily Beast, and other publications. Over the past two weeks, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft have outlined plans to spend more than $740 billion on capital expenditures this year, which Wall Street is reading as AI infrastructure spending, including data centers and chips.

Earlier in the AI boom, investors largely rewarded such big outlays, viewing them as a sign of confidence in the technology’s growth potential. But as we enter the fourth quarter, that enthusiasm seems to be giving way to concerns about negative free cash flow (spending more cash than a company brings in), mounting debt, and whether these enormous investments will ever generate enough returns.

The anxiety spilled across the market on Friday. The Nasdaq fell 2.9%, and chip stocks took a drubbing, too: Nvidia dropped 4%, Broadcom more than 5%, and Qualcomm 11%. Alphabet, which plummeted 12% on Thursday, its worst day on record, wiping out $500 billion in market value, fell again.

A big part of the concern is that companies that used to have overflowing free cash flow from their core businesses are getting hit as AI threatens the economics of those businesses. Alphabet provided the clearest example of that this week. Google’s parent company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the third quarter, its second consecutive quarter in the red, even as quarterly capex grew to $51.4 billion. Alphabet expects to spend up to $205 billion this year, and expects that spending to keep rising in 2027.

Meanwhile, the wild success of AI Mode — Google’s AI-powered chatbot feature built directly into Search — is eating into the company’s money-maker. Google’s Search advertising business, which makes up roughly half of its revenue, saw growth slow to 12%, its weakest pace in five quarters. That leaves Google walking a tightrope. It’s spending billions on the AI technology that could undermine the search business that pays it.

Amazon is in a similar boat after reporting negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with $14.8 billion in positive free cash flow the year before. The company says it expects to spend $220 billion in capex this year. Even though revenue at its cloud business, AWS, grew 39%, Amazon’s stock tumbled 7% after it reported earnings Thursday.

Meta is also burning cash, reporting negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in the third quarter as capex outpaced its operating cash. It’s guiding to as much as $145 billion in capex this year. The company noted that Muse, its new free personal AI agent, is a bit of a money pit (it’s “very compute-intensive to run,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said). But ad revenue grew 26%. Microsoft was the only exception when it came to free cash flow — it recorded $18.6 billion in positive free cash flow in its latest quarter, with spending on capex at $45.2 billion, less than the $50 billion it projected. Microsoft said that wasn’t an intentional pullback from AI spending, blaming delays in capacity from third-party providers. As a result, shares of smaller companies that rent out AI computing power sank .

It’s worth noting that the money to pay for all of this AI infrastructure isn’t just coming from the Big Tech companies’ profits. It’s also showing up in stock and bond sales. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle raised a combined $326 billion in debt in 2026, triple the amount raised last year.
Demand for AI compute remains strong. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft all saw gains in their cloud businesses. But investors are getting spooked by the costs of meeting that demand.

These muddied waters could complicate Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO. The AI company filed to go public earlier this week, and its future growth depends on securing enormous amounts of compute. Financial Times reported Friday that Blackstone has warned investors the company might not qualify for an investment-grade rating after its IPO, meaning it might end up being more reliant on the hyperscalers and third-parties to fund its infrastructure ambitions.

sources.title: Cracks emerge in AI borrowing boom as CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank debt worries grow - The Business Times
passages: The broader question is whether companies facing debt trouble like CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank are the industry’s weak links or are harbingers of deeper problems in the AI build-out.
Investors have sold off bonds for other AI giants as well, including Larry Ellison’s company, Oracle, though the price declines are not as steep as CoreWeave’s.
Not every data centre developer worries bond investors equally.
The larger so-called hyperscalers, such as Meta and Alphabet, which continue to borrow heavily, have been forced by investors to pay only modestly more in interest in recent debt deals.
The cost of insuring against losses on SoftBank’s debt has spiked.
It now costs more than US$40,000 to insure against US$1 million of SoftBank debt.
At the beginning of 2026, the cost was less than US$27,000.
Those questions burst into the forefront this past week when investors rapidly lost confidence in one debt-laden data centre company, CoreWeave.

Prices of its bonds – the company has accrued US$72 billion in liabilities to operate 51 data centres – crashed, and investors placed a more than 60 per cent likelihood that CoreWeave would fail to meet its obligations.
Oracle has faced slowdowns on multiple projects.
SoftBank has borrowed heavily to make one of the biggest bets – by dollar value – on OpenAI.
The Japanese conglomerate, led by Masayoshi Son, wrote its first US$500 million check in 2024 and a year later invested US$30 billion more.
That is just a year before Oracle’s debt comes due.
Some of the debt has traded around US$0.90 on the US dollar or below that, according to two traders, a steep drop for a relatively new loan.
CoreWeave’s business model defies easy description.
Its financial arrangements have been compared by some investors and analysts with those of the troubled office-space provider WeWork.
Oracle planned to pay back the borrowed money on the Texas facility helped by profits from the latter complex, called Project Lighthouse, which it expected to be operational by 2028.
In response to questions about SoftBank’s increasing debt, Alex Clavel, CEO of the SoftBank Vision Funds, said the amount of debt as a percentage of SoftBank Group’s assets had not changed.
TRILLIONS of dollars in borrowed money have powered the artificial intelligence boom.
First, CoreWeave buys Nvidia and other AI chips.
Then, as with WeWork, which leases space inside office buildings owned by others, CoreWeave contracts with data centre owners to use the structures for AI computing for 15 years or more.
CoreWeave then sub-leases the space to customers, including Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI, for a shorter time frame.
Several investors said they worried about whether hyperscalers like Meta and Microsoft would even need to lease space from CoreWeave in the future.
Alternately, they are wary of whether the data centres could become dated or even obsolete as their existing contracts expire.
Oracle faces similar permitting issues at a data centre project in New Mexico.
The project’s developer, investment firm Blue Owl, has started construction on the facility, but Oracle is struggling to get state permits to provide enough power.

The rub is that CoreWeave is on the hook for costs on both ends: It must pay to assemble and operate the facilities before any tenant is in place, and it is committed to the space for longer than its customers may stick around.

passages: TRILLIONS of dollars in borrowed money have powered the artificial intelligence boom. But now there is growing uncertainty around just how easily more money can be obtained – and how much of it will be paid back.

Those questions burst into the forefront this past week when investors rapidly lost confidence in one debt-laden data centre company, CoreWeave. Prices of its bonds – the company has accrued US$72 billion in liabilities to operate 51 data centres – crashed, and investors placed a more than 60 per cent likelihood that CoreWeave would fail to meet its obligations.
Investors have sold off bonds for other AI giants as well, including Larry Ellison’s company, Oracle, though the price declines are not as steep as CoreWeave’s.

At the same time, Wall Street investors have been bidding up the price of some complicated financial instruments that insure corporate debt against default, like those insuring SoftBank, the Japanese technology colossus that has borrowed heavily to bet its future on a partnership with OpenAI.

The recent market moves could spell losses for investors that own the companies’ existing bonds and could mean the companies will be forced to pay higher interest rates when they borrow again, raising the costs of their already wildly expensive AI projects.
The broader question is whether companies facing debt trouble like CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank are the industry’s weak links or are harbingers of deeper problems in the AI build-out.
Five decades of milestones and moments that shaped Singapore’s success story - told through our headlines.

The spread, or extra premium that investors demand to put their money into risky AI debt investments, has shot up more than 50 per cent over the past six months, according to Barclays, the investment bank.
“The market is on a knife’s edge everywhere,” said Alexandra Coleman, founder of Azraq, a data centre risk researcher.

A lot is riding on the continuation of the borrowing binge. Every week lately, economists, banks and private equity firms project higher and higher amounts of debt that they say will be needed to finance the AI systems that their boosters assert will run the world in a few years.

Virtually every major mutual fund company, insurer and private equity firm has been buying up the AI debt, to say nothing of the scores of individual investors who have poured money into skyrocketing AI companies.

Not every data centre developer worries bond investors equally. The larger so-called hyperscalers, such as Meta and Alphabet, which continue to borrow heavily, have been forced by investors to pay only modestly more in interest in recent debt deals. Investors have also sold out of some these companies’ existing debt, though the drop in bond prices has been less steep than for CoreWeave.
CoreWeave’s business model defies easy description. Its financial arrangements have been compared by some investors and analysts with those of the troubled office-space provider WeWork.

First, CoreWeave buys Nvidia and other AI chips. Then, as with WeWork, which leases space inside office buildings owned by others, CoreWeave contracts with data centre owners to use the structures for AI computing for 15 years or more. CoreWeave then sub-leases the space to customers, including Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI, for a shorter time frame.

The rub is that CoreWeave is on the hook for costs on both ends: It must pay to assemble and operate the facilities before any tenant is in place, and it is committed to the space for longer than its customers may stick around.

Several investors said they worried about whether hyperscalers like Meta and Microsoft would even need to lease space from CoreWeave in the future. Alternately, they are wary of whether the data centres could become dated or even obsolete as their existing contracts expire.

Another worry is the growing number of US data-centre projects being delayed by permitting issues or, in some cases, falling through.

Oracle has faced slowdowns on multiple projects. In 2025, the company easily borrowed US$38 billion from a group of banks to build, with the help of project developers, a pair of data centres, one in Texas and another on about 809 hectares of farmland in Port Washington, Wisconsin.

Aterio, a data centre researcher, said it was looking less likely that Project Lighthouse’s four data centres would start operating before 2029.
That is just a year before Oracle’s debt comes due. Some of the debt has traded around US$0.90 on the US dollar or below that, according to two traders, a steep drop for a relatively new loan.

Oracle faces similar permitting issues at a data centre project in New Mexico. The project’s developer, investment firm Blue Owl, has started construction on the facility, but Oracle is struggling to get state permits to provide enough power.
Some of the US$18 billion in debt tied to the project has recently sold at steep discounts, roughly US$0.80 on the US dollar, according to two people familiar with the trades.

SoftBank has borrowed heavily to make one of the biggest bets – by dollar value – on OpenAI. The Japanese conglomerate, led by Masayoshi Son, wrote its first US$500 million check in 2024 and a year later invested US$30 billion more.
To get that money, Son sold off most of SoftBank’s holdings of Nvidia and T-Mobile and took out loans against his stake in chip designer Arm Holdings.

In 2026, Son invested again. On Oct 1, SoftBank completed another US$30 billion investment in OpenAI. Before doing so, in late September the company raised a record US$11 billion in debt at interest rates of nearly 10 per cent.
In response to questions about SoftBank’s increasing debt, Alex Clavel, CEO of the SoftBank Vision Funds, said the amount of debt as a percentage of SoftBank Group’s assets had not changed.

sources.title: AI spending is soaring, but where is the revenue? Anand Shah flags cracks in the boom
passages: Anand Shah, CIO of PMS & AIF at ICICI Prudential AMC, sees cracks emerging in the artificial intelligence investment boom as revenue generation fails to keep pace with spending on infrastructure.
He believes the sustainability of the massive investment cycle will depend on how effectively AI companies convert spending into revenue.“Today, the boom is in AI investment.

We are not seeing a big boom in terms of revenue,” Shah told CNBC-TV18 in an interview.He pointed to pressure on companies supplying AI infrastructure, including chip manufacturers and businesses benefiting from electrification, alongside revenue concerns among AI companies.

He argued that the country would continue to need foreign direct investment and foreign institutional investor flows unless exports increased significantly relative to imports.Shah also noted that the securities transaction tax had become a source of revenue for the government, while saying the future direction of equity taxation remained uncertain.“We need to be mindful that, unlike many other economies that run surpluses, exporting more than they consume or producing more than they consume, India is much more dependent on foreign flows,” he said.He added that attracting foreign investment would remain important until India built sufficient manufacturing strength to export substantially more than it does today.Watch accompanying video for full conversation.

Shah expects the resulting revenue growth to create operating leverage, with additional capital expenditure and expenses remaining relatively limited compared with the opportunity.India needs foreign investment until exports strengthenOn equity taxation, Shah said India needed to remain mindful of its dependence on foreign investment flows to fund its deficit.

Shah said the emerging weakness challenged the broader narrative that a massive AI build-out would eventually disrupt and wipe out several other industries.Anand Shah starts adding to IT stocks after prolonged underweight positionDespite concerns about AI disruption, Shah sees a potential opportunity for Indian IT services companies as businesses move towards integrating AI into their operations.ICICI Prudential AMC has started increasing its exposure to IT stocks after remaining underweight for a prolonged period, although the fund house will remain marginally underweight for now.“The next leg is when we will gain the confidence to increase our weightages,” Shah said.He said IT companies had been cutting prices and passing on a significant part of the benefits from AI to customers while still managing their top line. As companies seek to integrate AI into their systems, IT services providers could benefit from the implementation work. Greater confidence in the sector's performance could prompt the fund house to increase its allocation further.Why ICICI Prudential AMC prefers manufacturing stocksShah said ICICI Prudential AMC remained overweight on manufacturing across large-, mid- and small-cap stocks, pointing to improving earnings and a changing competitive environment for Indian businesses competing with China.He said Indian manufacturers had faced pressure from Chinese competition for 15-20 years, but the situation was changing at the margin. Measures in China to curb excessive competition had also contributed to price increases in sectors such as chemicals.Metals offered another indication of the opportunity, with earnings growth of more than 30% over the previous few quarters, according to Shah. He also highlighted strong cash-flow generation, while cautioning that metal stocks remained inherently cyclical and volatile.Indian metal companies could benefit from having costs in rupees and revenues linked to the dollar, alongside access to resources such as iron ore, bauxite and coal. Shah added that rupee depreciation against the Chinese yuan had created a tailwind for Indian manufacturers competing with China, while making Chinese goods and raw materials more expensive for Indian buyers.Consumer companies face rising costs and tougher competitionIn contrast to manufacturing, Shah said consumer-facing businesses were dealing with higher input costs and intensifying competition, making it harder for companies to protect profitability.He pointed to the paint industry, where the number of major players had increased from four to seven or eight. The transition from 4G to 5G has been slower than the earlier shift from 3G to 4G because fewer immediate use cases have developed, he said. story.title: Cracks are emerging in the AI spending boom

facts.text: Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft have outlined more than $740 billion in capital spending this year, exposing cracks emerging spending boom as investors question the cost of AI infrastructure.
The spending boom is also being financed through borrowing and securities sales, not only through profits.
For investors, that question now sits alongside the companies’ latest cash-flow figures and spending plans.
The English-language global edition of JournalArta.
The broader question is whether companies facing debt trouble like CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank are the industry’s weak links or are harbingers of deeper problems in the AI build-out.
Investors have sold off bonds for other AI giants as well, including Larry Ellison’s company, Oracle, though the price declines are not as steep as CoreWeave’s.
Not every data centre developer worries bond investors equally.
The larger so-called hyperscalers, such as Meta and Alphabet, which continue to borrow heavily, have been forced by investors to pay only modestly more in interest in recent debt deals.
The cost of insuring against losses on SoftBank’s debt has spiked.
It now costs more than US$40,000 to insure against US$1 million of SoftBank debt.
At the beginning of 2026, the cost was less than US$27,000.

The Japanese conglomerate, led by Masayoshi Son, wrote its first US$500 million check in 2024 and a year later invested US$30 billion more.

extraction.body: Investors are getting nervous about AI infrastructure spending just as the Big Tech companies double down. Over the past two weeks, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft have outlined plans to spend more than $740 billion on capital expenditures this year, which Wall Street is reading as AI infrastructure spending, including data centers and chips. Earlier in the AI boom, investors largely rewarded such big outlays, viewing them as a sign of confidence in the technology’s growth potential. But as we enter the fourth quarter, that enthusiasm seems to be giving way to concerns about negative free cash flow (spending more cash than a company brings in), mounting debt, and whether these enormous investments will ever generate enough returns. The anxiety spilled across the market on Friday. The Nasdaq fell 2.9%, and chip stocks took a drubbing, too: Nvidia dropped 4%, Broadcom more than 5%, and Qualcomm 11%. Alphabet, which plummeted 12% on Thursday, its worst day on record, wiping out $500 billion in market value, fell again. A big part of the concern is that companies that used to have overflowing free cash flow from their core businesses are getting hit as AI threatens the economics of those businesses. Alphabet provided the clearest example of that this week. Google’s parent company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the third quarter, its second consecutive quarter in the red, even as quarterly capex grew to $51.4 billion. Alphabet expects to spend up to $205 billion this year, and expects that spending to keep rising in 2027. Meanwhile, the wild success of AI Mode — Google’s AI-powered chatbot feature built directly into Search — is eating into the company’s money-maker. Google’s Search advertising business, which makes up roughly half of its revenue, saw growth slow to 12%, its weakest pace in five quarters. That leaves Google walking a tightrope. It’s spending billions on the AI technology that could undermine the search business that pays it. Amazon is in a similar boat after reporting negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with $14.8 billion in positive free cash flow the year before. The company says it expects to spend $220 billion in capex this year. Even though revenue at its cloud business, AWS, grew 39%, Amazon’s stock tumbled 7% after it reported earnings Thursday. Meta is also burning cash, reporting negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in the third quarter as capex outpaced its operating cash. It’s guiding to as much as $145 billion in capex this year. The company noted that Muse, its new free personal AI agent, is a bit of a money pit (it’s “very compute-intensive to run,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said). But ad revenue grew 26%. Still, no amount of good news saved Meta from taking a 10% hit on its stock last week. Microsoft was the only exception when it came to free cash flow — it recorded $18.6 billion in positive free cash flow in its latest quarter, with spending on capex at $45.2 billion, less than the $50 billion it projected. Microsoft said that wasn’t an intentional pullback from AI spending, blaming delays in capacity from third-party providers. As a result, shares of smaller companies that rent out AI computing power sank . It’s worth noting that the money to pay for all of this AI infrastructure isn’t just coming from the Big Tech companies’ profits. It’s also showing up in stock and bond sales. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle raised a combined $326 billion in debt in 2026, triple the amount raised last year. Demand for AI compute remains strong. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft all saw gains in their cloud businesses. But investors are getting spooked by the costs of meeting that demand. These muddied waters could complicate Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO. The AI company filed to go public earlier this week, and its future growth depends on securing enormous amounts of compute. Financial Times reported Friday that Blackstone has warned investors the company might not qualify for an investment-grade rating after its IPO, meaning it might end up being more reliant on the hyperscalers and third-parties to fund its infrastructure ambitions. Rebecca Bellan is a senior reporter at TechCrunch where she covers the business, policy, and emerging trends shaping artificial intelligence. Her work has also appeared in Forbes, Bloomberg, The Atlantic, The Daily Beast, and other publications. sources.title: AI spending is soaring, but where is the revenue? Anand Shah flags cracks in the boom
passages: Anand Shah, CIO of PMS & AIF at ICICI Prudential AMC, sees cracks emerging in the artificial intelligence investment boom as revenue generation fails to keep pace with spending on infrastructure.
He believes the sustainability of the massive investment cycle will depend on how effectively AI companies convert spending into revenue.“Today, the boom is in AI investment.

We are not seeing a big boom in terms of revenue,” Shah told CNBC-TV18 in an interview.He pointed to pressure on companies supplying AI infrastructure, including chip manufacturers and businesses benefiting from electrification, alongside revenue concerns among AI companies.

He argued that the country would continue to need foreign direct investment and foreign institutional investor flows unless exports increased significantly relative to imports.Shah also noted that the securities transaction tax had become a source of revenue for the government, while saying the future direction of equity taxation remained uncertain.“We need to be mindful that, unlike many other economies that run surpluses, exporting more than they consume or producing more than they consume, India is much more dependent on foreign flows,” he said.He added that attracting foreign investment would remain important until India built sufficient manufacturing strength to export substantially more than it does today.Watch accompanying video for full conversation.

Shah expects the resulting revenue growth to create operating leverage, with additional capital expenditure and expenses remaining relatively limited compared with the opportunity.India needs foreign investment until exports strengthenOn equity taxation, Shah said India needed to remain mindful of its dependence on foreign investment flows to fund its deficit.

He believes the sustainability of the massive investment cycle will depend on how effectively AI companies convert spending into revenue.“Today, the boom is in AI investment. We are not seeing a big boom in terms of revenue,” Shah told CNBC-TV18 in an interview.He pointed to pressure on companies supplying AI infrastructure, including chip manufacturers and businesses benefiting from electrification, alongside revenue concerns among AI companies. Shah said the emerging weakness challenged the broader narrative that a massive AI build-out would eventually disrupt and wipe out several other industries.Anand Shah starts adding to IT stocks after prolonged underweight positionDespite concerns about AI disruption, Shah sees a potential opportunity for Indian IT services companies as businesses move towards integrating AI into their operations.ICICI Prudential AMC has started increasing its exposure to IT stocks after remaining underweight for a prolonged period, although the fund house will remain marginally underweight for now.“The next leg is when we will gain the confidence to increase our weightages,” Shah said.He said IT companies had been cutting prices and passing on a significant part of the benefits from AI to customers while still managing their top line. As companies seek to integrate AI into their systems, IT services providers could benefit from the implementation work. Greater confidence in the sector's performance could prompt the fund house to increase its allocation further.Why ICICI Prudential AMC prefers manufacturing stocksShah said ICICI Prudential AMC remained overweight on manufacturing across large-, mid- and small-cap stocks, pointing to improving earnings and a changing competitive environment for Indian businesses competing with China.He said Indian manufacturers had faced pressure from Chinese competition for 15-20 years, but the situation was changing at the margin. Measures in China to curb excessive competition had also contributed to price increases in sectors such as chemicals.Metals offered another indication of the opportunity, with earnings growth of more than 30% over the previous few quarters, according to Shah. He also highlighted strong cash-flow generation, while cautioning that metal stocks remained inherently cyclical and volatile.Indian metal companies could benefit from having costs in rupees and revenues linked to the dollar, alongside access to resources such as iron ore, bauxite and coal. Shah added that rupee depreciation against the Chinese yuan had created a tailwind for Indian manufacturers competing with China, while making Chinese goods and raw materials more expensive for Indian buyers.Consumer companies face rising costs and tougher competitionIn contrast to manufacturing, Shah said consumer-facing businesses were dealing with higher input costs and intensifying competition, making it harder for companies to protect profitability.He pointed to the paint industry, where the number of major players had increased from four to seven or eight. The transition from 4G to 5G has been slower than the earlier shift from 3G to 4G because fewer immediate use cases have developed, he said. Shah expects the resulting revenue growth to create operating leverage, with additional capital expenditure and expenses remaining relatively limited compared with the opportunity.India needs foreign investment until exports strengthenOn equity taxation, Shah said India needed to remain mindful of its dependence on foreign investment flows to fund its deficit. sources.title: Why bitcoin held up better after the record Binance hack - CNBC
passages: "Investors recognize an important distinction: Bitcoin itself was not hacked," Callahan told CNBC.
"This was a security breach at a centralized exchange, not a failure of the Bitcoin network."

"The speed of Binance's response, its deep financial resources, and its assurances that no user funds would be lost have helped restore market confidence and prevent potential panic," Hallarn told CNBC.
Binance has suffered the biggest hack in crypto history , but that's done little to shake confidence in bitcoin , according to market analysts and researchers.

"We believe Binance has more than enough liquidity to cover the hole and we expect the exchange to remain solvent while reimbursing user funds," Compass Point analyst Ed Engel said Friday in a note to clients.
The hack sparked a slight sell-off in bitcoin .
Gox was hacked a handful of times, wreaking havoc on the price of bitcoin.
Binance also has a $1.2 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users to offset losses from security breaches and other events.
The firm could also be eligible for loans that would minimize its solvency risks, if history is any indication, according to investment bank Compass Point.
Binance said it has started recovering affected assets, which has likely assuaged some of investors' concerns, according to Spencer Hallarn, head of markets at crypto trading firm GSR.
Just 6% of bitcoin is held in exchange-traded funds, according to data from bitcoin analytics platform Bitbo.
That suggests many bitcoins are still being held by long-term believers in the asset and its cypherpunk origins, Lawant said.

The hack sparked a slight sell-off in bitcoin . On Friday, the cryptocurrency traded at $77,065 around 1:34 p.m. ET, down about 4% on the day. By comparison, the token has fallen 8.3% on average in the first 24 hours following past crypto exchange exploits, according to data from institutional crypto platform Anchorage Digital. The digital asset has remained relatively resilient because the hack on Binance had nothing to do with the security of the bitcoin network itself, according to Sam Callahan, director of bitcoin strategy and research at crypto treasury firm OranjeBTC. "Investors recognize an important distinction: Bitcoin itself was not hacked," Callahan told CNBC. "This was a security breach at a centralized exchange, not a failure of the Bitcoin network." Although Binance has suffered the largest hack in crypto history, it's far from the only digital asset exchange to fall victim to bad actors and lead bitcoin to tumble. In the early 2010s, bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox was hacked a handful of times, wreaking havoc on the price of bitcoin. The token fell as much as 23.7% in the first 24 hours after an attack on Mt. Gox in February 2014, per Anchorage Digital data. More recently, crypto exchange Bybit suffered roughly $1.5 billion in losses due to an exploit targeting its trading platform. Last month, crypto platform Bitget was drained of more than $350 million in digital assets. What's different about the Binance hack is that it hasn't sparked the same loss in confidence in crypto markets that occurred after other major crypto security incidents, according to Spencer Hallarn, head of markets at crypto trading firm GSR. "The speed of Binance's response, its deep financial resources, and its assurances that no user funds would be lost have helped restore market confidence and prevent potential panic," Hallarn told CNBC. Tether, Circle and several other crypto firms said they had frozen roughly $3 billion in funds stolen in the heist. That should help mitigate losses tied to the attack, the executive noted. Binance also has a $1.2 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users to offset losses from security breaches and other events. The firm could also be eligible for loans that would minimize its solvency risks, if history is any indication, according to investment bank Compass Point. "We believe Binance has more than enough liquidity to cover the hole and we expect the exchange to remain solvent while reimbursing user funds," Compass Point analyst Ed Engel said Friday in a note to clients. "ByBit also received a bridge loan after its $1.5bn hack last year; therefore, we believe Binance has financing options." GSR's Hallarn noted that this latest rotation out of technology stocks may also be to blame for some of the pressure on bitcoin. "Since the exploit, bitcoin has largely traded in lockstep with other risk assets, including equities, which sold off overnight amid concerns over AI-related earnings," Hallarn told CNBC. The iShares A.I. Innovation and Tech Active ETF (BAI) was down more than 8% on the day. Still, Anchorage Digital head of research David Lawant noted that current holders of bitcoin are more likely to hold their tokens through short-term headwinds than holders of other risk-on assets at the moment. extraction.body: Bitcoin has held up better than expected following the $6.3 billion Binance hack, according to Strive CEO Matt Cole, who said the breach does not undermine the cryptocurrency’s long-term investment thesis. Speaking on Cointelegraph’s Chain Reaction on Friday, Cole said the breach had not changed his long-term investment case for Bitcoin. He compared the attack on Binance’s wallets to a bank robbery rather than a failure of Bitcoin’s network. Bitcoin traded near $77,400 at 4:00 pm on Saturday, about 4% below its price shortly before the attack began Thursday, according to CoinGecko data. Strive, a publicly traded company that holds Bitcoin on its balance sheet, reported owning 43,000 BTC as of Oct. 23. “I do have conviction that over any reasonable time frame, this does not change the investment thesis on Bitcoin,” Cole said. Cole said Bitcoin’s decline was less severe than he expected given the scale of the breach and broader market weakness, although he acknowledged that it was too early to determine whether the cryptocurrency had reached a price bottom. Cole described the market as being in an “early spring” recovery phase that could last another six to nine months, with prices gradually rising rather than surging to new highs. Paul Chapman, financial crime director at Wirex, also distinguished the attack on Binance from a compromise of Bitcoin’s network. “It’s important to be clear that Bitcoin itself hasn’t been hacked — this was an attack on one company’s systems, not the network,” he told Cointelegraph. According to Glassnode, Thursday’s Binance breach was the largest cryptocurrency hack on record, with around $6.3 billion affected, exceeding the combined losses from the next nine largest hacks. The previous record was the $1.5 billion Bybit exploit in February 2025. Glassnode said three of the 10 largest crypto hacks have occurred since the beginning of 2025, all involving exchanges. Binance hack exceeds the next nine largest crypto exploits combined. Source: Glassnode By comparison, following the Bybit hack in 2025, Bitcoin fell roughly 5% from nearly $100,000 to around $95,000 amid the breach and broader market volatility, according to a Bitfinex market report. Anchorage Digital data cited by CNBC put Bitcoin’s average decline in the first 24 hours after previous crypto exchange exploits at 8.3%. Binance hack exposes exchange security vulnerabilities Blockaid CEO Ido Ben-Natan said the attackers appeared to have compromised Binance’s transaction signing process. Binance said Friday that it had found no evidence of leaked wallet private keys, though its investigation remained ongoing. Blockaid’s analysis identified an Ethereum transaction containing 50 signed authorizations covering different transaction counts. A matching authorization allowed attacker-controlled code to operate through the wallet. Ben-Natan argued that checks before signing could have blocked the malicious authorization. The North Korean link will send claims teams straight to their wordings. Under Lloyd’s Market Bulletin Y5381 , standalone cyber policies written at Lloyd’s since 31 March 2023 must exclude two things. The first is war. The second is any state-backed attack that significantly impairs a state’s ability to function or its security capabilities. The bulletin also requires each policy to set out a robust basis for attributing an attack to a state.

That test is aimed at attacks with national-scale consequences. Whether a theft from a private exchange meets it is open to argument, and wordings vary between policies. Brokers have warned of grey areas since the mandate was announced. Clear Group’s George Grimshaw has told Insurance Business that cyber cover is “not going to cover anything when it comes to war or state-backed attacks”. Under war exclusions, the insurer generally carries the burden of proving the exclusion applies.

Formal attribution will matter. After the Bybit theft, the FBI named TraderTraitor within a week. A similar statement this time would strengthen the hand of any insurer arguing that the loss was state-backed.

The FCA published its final cryptoasset rules on 30 June. Its authorisation gateway opened on 30 September and closes on 28 February 2027, and the regime comes into force on 25 October 2027. PwC’s summary says that firms involved in trading, custody, intermediation and staking will all need authorisation.

The senior managers and certification regime is part of the new framework. Directors of newly authorised crypto firms will therefore carry personal accountability, which is likely to make them look harder at D&O cover. All this is happening while the market absorbs the largest crypto loss on record. Lloyd’s had already warned that rapid cyber growth may be outstripping the market’s capacity to absorb risk .
Read next: Lloyd’s new cyber mandate spurs “grey area” fears
The Binance breach follows Bitget’s loss of roughly US$350m in September. TRM Labs says North Korea-linked groups took about 76% of all crypto hack value in the first four months of 2026.

Prices fell overnight. Bitcoin dropped more than 3% to a six-week low, and BNB, Binance’s own token, fell between 5% and 8%. Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group, told Reuters the breach could prompt investors to reassess counterparty, solvency and liquidity risk at centralised exchanges.

Kevin March, co-founder of JPEG Trading, told The Wall Street Journal he expected Binance to manage the loss. Its rivals are watching. Few exchanges hold reserves that could absorb a single loss on this scale.
This story is developing and will be updated.

extraction.body: Cole's comments came in an interview on Cointelegraph 's Chain Reaction on Friday. During the aftermath of the hack, Bitcoin traded around $77,400 as of Saturday at 4:00 pm, according to CoinGecko price data-about 4% below its level shortly before the Thursday incident began. Cole said the scale of the Binance breach had not changed his long-term view of Bitcoin. In his framing, the attack resembles a bank robbery-something that can happen to a particular institution-rather than evidence that the broader financial system has stopped working. He also suggested the market decline was less severe than he expected given both the magnitude of the hack and wider weakness across crypto markets. At the same time, Cole acknowledged that it was too early to determine whether Bitcoin had reached a durable price bottom. Looking ahead, Cole described the market as being in an“early spring” recovery phase that could persist for another six to nine months. Rather than expecting a rapid re-test of all-time highs, he said the more likely path is gradual improvement over time. For context on why Cole's perspective carries weight, Strive is a publicly traded firm that holds Bitcoin on its balance sheet. The company reported owning 43,000 BTC as of Oct. 23, per the figures referenced in the report. Several participants in the coverage emphasized the same distinction: the Binance breach did not equal a compromise of Bitcoin's core network. Wirex 's financial crime director Paul Chapman drew a sharp line between attacks on a company's internal systems and an actual hack of the cryptocurrency protocol. “It's important to be clear that Bitcoin itself hasn't been hacked - this was an attack on one company's systems, not the network,” Chapman told Cointelegraph. That distinction matters for investors because it separates two types of risk: platform-level operational and custody vulnerabilities on one hand, and systemic risks to the blockchain on the other. Even when the market reacts strongly to exchange incidents, analysts and executives typically treat these events as reminders to reassess counterparty safety, wallet management, and signing processes-rather than as evidence that Bitcoin's consensus is broken. According to Glassnode, Thursday's Binance breach was the largest cryptocurrency hack on record, with around $6.3 billion affected-more than the combined losses from the next nine largest crypto hacks. Glassnode also noted that three of the 10 largest crypto hacks occurred since the beginning of 2025, and each involved exchanges. The earlier record referenced in the reporting was the $1.5 billion Bybit exploit in February 2025. The comparison is instructive because it shows how exchange-driven disruptions have repeatedly shaped short-term price action without necessarily changing long-term network assumptions. After the Bybit hack, Bitcoin fell about 5% from nearly $100,000 to around $95,000 during the period of breach-related volatility, according to a Bitfinex market report. Additional context comes from data Anchorage Digital cited by CNBC, which put Bitcoin's average decline in the first 24 hours after previous crypto exchange exploits at 8.3%. In that light, the post-Binance drawdown observed in the immediate trading window-around 4% from before the incident began at the time the Saturday reading was recorded-appears comparatively milder, though traders will still be watching whether broader risk conditions worsen or stabilize. While the market focus is often on headlines and price swings, technical reporting in the coverage underscored that the nature of the breach is crucial for understanding where defenses failed. Blockaid CEO Ido Ben-Natan said the attackers appeared to have compromised Binance's transaction signing process. Binance, according to the coverage, said it had found no evidence of leaked wallet private keys, though its investigation was ongoing. Ben-Natan's analysis, as reported, described an Ethereum transaction that contained 50 signed authorizations tied to different transaction counts. A matching authorization reportedly enabled attacker-controlled code to execute through the wallet. Ben-Natan argued that checks before signing could have prevented the malicious authorization from being approved. Whether or not Binance's implementation details ultimately align with that interpretation, the takeaway for builders and users is clear: even without leaked private keys, systems that authorize transactions through software signing flows can still be attacked if safeguards are insufficient. For the months ahead, the key thing market participants will watch is whether Bitcoin's stabilization after the Binance incident proves durable-Cole suggested a gradual recovery window-alongside whether exchanges accelerate improvements in signing, authorization controls, and incident transparency. Until investigators close remaining gaps, the biggest uncertainty is less about Bitcoin's network integrity and more about how quickly the broader industry can reduce the likelihood of similar failures.
