extraction.body: Salt and vinegar chips, in my opinion, are one of the most divisive snacks out there. People either love that sharp, acidic punch or want absolutely nothing to do with it.I am firmly in the first camp, which is why I rounded up every bag I could find to see which brand makes the best ones. My ideal salt and vinegar chip is so aggressively vinegary that it practically makes my eyes water, but for this taste test, I tried to show a little restraint. The best chip is balanced: enough acidity to make your mouth pucker, plenty of salt, a strong potato flavor, and, most importantly, a chip sturdy enough to handle it all.I tried seven popular brands—Lay’s, Siete, Utz, Kettle Brand, Cape Cod, Deep River, and Pringles—to find the one that does salt and vinegar best. Instead of that clean, crisp crunch I want from a potato chip, these had an almost powdery quality that made each bite feel oddly dry. It built quickly into a harsh sourness that became almost nauseating after a few chips.Looking at the ingredient list, the seasoning relies on sodium diacetate along with several acids, and I could really taste that concentrated acidity. I love a powerful salt and vinegar chip, but this one crossed the line from punchy into overwhelming.6. PringlesPringles Salt Vinegar taste exactly like what you would expect: a familiar Pringles base with a tangy layer of vinegar seasoning.The flavor is pleasant, with a mild acidic bite and enough salt to make it clearly salt and vinegar. For this particular flavor, I want an actual potato chip with enough heft and crunch to stand up against all that acidity—not a potato-based crisp.If you already love Pringles, you’ll probably enjoy these. These have a great, substantial crunch, and the avocado oil imparts a mild flavor that lets the potato shine.What I didn't like was the serrano. The added pepper brings a mild vegetal heat that competes with the vinegar instead of letting it be the star. A noticeable salty tang still comes through, but I kept wishing I could taste more of it without the serrano getting in the way.Still, the crunch and vinegar were good enough to land these safely above the bottom two.4. Lay’sLay’s were a definite step up for me.The thin chip is light and crispy, and the potato itself tastes better than Utz. The seasoning has a clean, familiar salt and vinegar flavor with a pleasant sharpness that hits right away.I just wanted more of it.For a flavor this bold, Lay’s felt a little too polite. The vinegar fades quickly, leaving you mostly with the salty potato chip underneath. These are extremely easy to eat, but if I’m buying salt and vinegar chips, I want the vinegar to make itself known.3. Deep RiverDeep River delivered the first truly satisfying vinegar punch of the group.The acidity hits immediately, but it comes across slightly sweeter and rounder than some of the sharper chips in this ranking. That little touch of sweetness softens the sourness without eliminating it, and the seasoning lingers nicely after each bite.The kettle-cooked texture also gives these the sturdy crunch this flavor needs. They weren’t quite as balanced as my top two, but I appreciated that Deep River wasn’t afraid of vinegar.2. Kettle BrandKettle Brand came extremely close to taking the top spot. The chips have a fantastic crunch: thick and substantial without becoming painfully hard. The vinegar flavor is bright, acidic, and immediately satisfying, with enough salt to make the whole thing pop.My only complaint is how quickly the seasoning disappears. The first few seconds of each bite are exactly what I want from salt and vinegar, but once that initial tang fades, you’re mostly left with a plain potato chip.Apparently that didn’t bother me too much, because I kept reaching back into the bag. Cape CodCape Cod gave me the best overall combination of crunch, salt, potato, and vinegar.These have a bold kettle-cooked crunch that immediately makes them feel more substantial, followed by a vinegar flavor that is bright and tangy without becoming harsh. I could personally handle even more acidity, but the balance here is what ultimately earned them first place.The seasoning includes both white vinegar and apple cider vinegar, and I think that combination really sets these apart. The white vinegar gives you that clean acidic bite, while the apple cider vinegar adds a slightly fruitier, more rounded tang that gives the overall flavor more depth.Delish Test Kitchen Manager Alejandro Valdes Lora agreed, praising the great texture and fresh, crisp, slightly oily potato-chip flavor. He even went so far as to declare that Cape Cod “never disappoints.” I couldn’t agree more.After eating my way through seven bags, one thing became very clear: Kettle-cooked chips are the ideal vehicle for salt and vinegar. A flavor this strong needs a substantial potato chip underneath it. The thicker crunch gives all that sharp vinegar and salt something to push against, creating a much more satisfying bite.And while I will always support a chip acidic enough to make me tear up, Cape Cod proved that sometimes balance wins.

passages: The flavor on the Kettle Cooked Olive Oil Potato Chips is a bit more subtle than some others, which I like, but it's the texture that gives them a slight edge over the ridge-style kettle chips in my book.
The chips are thin and crispy rather than hefty thanks to thinly sliced potatoes.
I compare them to the (upcoming) white truffle chips as far as texture, but the olive oil gives these chips a very different flavor.
When ranking chips, I knew which ones from Trader Joe's were already popular in my household, but I also tried some new flavor options to compare.
While there are tried-and-true crispy options, specialty selections like white truffle and Carolina Gold barbecue stand out from the pack.
There are also a few different texture varieties, including multiple ridge cut styles and even a super crispy lattice cut chip.
They're budget-friendly, too, so even when I'm looking for the best value, there are always a couple of options to add to my cart.
The crunchy texture is the best part of these chips, especially if you like a thinner chip like I do.
These are perfect for snacking — they aren't really heavy or dense but still give you a little something to enjoy.
The flavor isn't anything spectacular, but they have enough salt to satisfy a craving.
They're made out of thick slices of potatoes that are cut into ridges, cooked in sunflower oil, and finally sprinkled with sea salt.
The ingredients list is super short, perfect for those who are keeping a close eye on additives or preservatives.
Thanks to the addition of sea salt, these have the salty taste that you come to expect from a good potato chip without overpowering.
The heat doesn't come close to the ghost pepper and is more smoky than spicy, so don't worry about it being too overpowering.
If you're serving these to kids, their clothing and your upholstery have a better chance of coming out unscathed if you keep napkins nearby.
The salty flavor here goes with just about anything, even if you'll probably end up with broken chips in your bowl.
I like to add them as a crunchy topping on a sandwich, smash them to use as a salty breading for chicken, or pour them into a snack bowl.
Versatility is another thing that I appreciate in a potato chip, since I rarely get through a whole bag before they start to get stale.
You can use these chips in so many ways and never grow tired of their wonderful flavor.
I was happy to see plenty of options at my local TJ's, but you can also call ahead to reserve your favorites if you want something specific.
They're similar to other saddle-style chips in both texture and taste but only come in classic original rather than the huge variety of flavors that you find from other brands.
I knew I was in for a delicious snack as soon as I opened the bag.
The super-rich flavor of the white truffle oil on each chip is decadent.
If there's such a thing as an elevated potato chip, these are it.
I've never tried another chip that has quite the same type of flavor.
They are sturdy enough to scoop up creamy homemade chip dips , which can also help tone down the heat.
If I'm going to eat more than a few, I'll typically have some sour cream dip nearby, which pairs well with the spiciness here.
It's made with a generous sprinkling of Everything but the Bagel, or E.B.T.B., seasoning .
They are my favorite because of the perfect blend of salty seasoning on an airy, crunchy chip.

extraction.body: Trader Joe's is known for its delicious, unique-flavored snacks, and its potato chips are no exception. While there are tried-and-true crispy options, specialty selections like white truffle and Carolina Gold barbecue stand out from the pack. There are also a few different texture varieties, including multiple ridge cut styles and even a super crispy lattice cut chip. They're budget-friendly, too, so even when I'm looking for the best value, there are always a couple of options to add to my cart. My snack strategy includes a classic chip that I know I'll like, such as ridges or salty favorites, as well as a new flavor or texture variety to spice things up — and I wanted to know which ones should be added to my rotation. While I relied on potato chip-eating expertise carefully honed through years of backyard barbecues, picnics, and brown-bagging it for school lunch, a side-by-side taste test provided the best opportunity to really compare all the chip offerings Trader Joe's has on its shelves. I was happy to see plenty of options at my local TJ's, but you can also call ahead to reserve your favorites if you want something specific. One of the things I love most about shopping at Trader Joe's is popping in to pick up something I've never tried before, and the chip aisle is bursting with new options all the time. Without any further ado, let's get ranking. Unless you really love hot and spicy, the Ghost Pepper Potato Chips will probably be a bit too much to eat regularly. While ghost peppers aren't the hottest pepper in the world , they still pack quite a kick. The first couple of bites are pleasantly hot and tingly, but after a few chips, my mouth started burning. Unlike some flavored chips, these don't have a strong scent, distinct color, or messy exterior seasoning. So while you don't need to worry about getting a lot of residue on your fingers as you eat them, it does make it easy to reach for these by mistake and get more spice than you expected. In all, they're a fun variation on a standard potato chip, but not one that I'll be grabbing often. The lattice-style cut is one of the crispier options for Trader Joe's chips and my favorite part about this chip. They are sturdy enough to scoop up creamy homemade chip dips , which can also help tone down the heat. If I'm going to eat more than a few, I'll typically have some sour cream dip nearby, which pairs well with the spiciness here. The saddle potato chips come in a convenient tube that keeps their shape intact, which makes them a great option if you're packing snacks for a trip. But otherwise, these chips are only okay, especially when you compare them to other flavorful options on the same shelf. They're similar to other saddle-style chips in both texture and taste but only come in classic original rather than the huge variety of flavors that you find from other brands. If you like saddle chips, these are the only option from Trader Joe's, but they aren't on my list of favorite potato chips overall. The chips themselves have plenty of salt, but it's in the form larger seat salt crystals that aren't coated on or embedded into the chip. Because of this, it usually comes right off as you eat. The sea salt does add some extra crunch but it can be inconsistent from chip to chip. They are also a bit pricey for the size, costing around $2 for just over 5 ounces of chips. Most other bagged chips from Trader Joe's are around $3 and can be twice as big or more. But thanks to the sturdy packaging, at least you know that the chips won't get smashed and you'll get to enjoy the entire container without too many crumbs left at the bottom. If you like everything bagel seasoning, you'll love the Everything but the Bagel chips from Trader Joe's. It's made with a generous sprinkling of Everything but the Bagel, or E.B.T.B., seasoning . extraction.body: Welcome to Dupe Detective, a column where I'll be reviewing a name brand food product's competitor product to find out how well it compares to, or even beats, the original. Despite a famously bold, sometimes mouth-numbing flavor, salt and vinegar chips are surprisingly versatile. Starbucks salt and vinegar chips, for example, can be paired with coffee for a combo as satisfying as it is unconventional. In another instance of chain restaurant chip innovation, Red Lobster once added salt and vinegar chips to breaded shrimp . Simply put, there's something distinctly gratifying about a robust vinegary tang amplified by almost too much salt on crispy potato that has inspired these and other adventurous eats. Kettle has arguably become one America's most beloved potato chip brands , producing what may well be the most iconic salt and vinegar chip available in grocery stores. Competing directly with Kettle Chips is Trader Joes, which sells Sea Salt & Vinegar Potato Chips with Avocado Oil. The Trader Joe's product even comes in a blue bag, reminiscent of the equivalent Kettle Chips packaging. I picked both brands' takes on the classic chip flavor from stores near my home in the suburbs of Las Vegas and tried them back-to-back. Ahead is a brief rundown of each item, before my thoughts on how Trader Joe's holds up against its name-brand competition. While the info isn't spotlighted on the front of the bag, Trader Joe's Sea Salt & Vinegar Potato Chips are, in fact, kettle-cooked. One of the foremost qualities that sets kettle-cooked chips apart from standard potato chips is their pronounced crunch, which is satisfying on its own, or even swapped into a nacho recipe for the crunchiest take on nachos possible. My Trader Joe's salt and vinegar chips were certainly crunchy, and I noticed they were the slightest bit thicker than the average potato chip too. In other words, I had nothing but positive thoughts about my Trader Joe's chips' texture. Foremost in my Trader Joe's Sea Salt & Vinegar Chips' flavor was malt vinegar. The fact I could taste that malty sweetness, more complex than a plain white vinegar, was a significant plus. Whereas some salt and vinegar chips are so bold they cause a tingling sensation from the get-go, I did notice a certain level of restraint from Trader Joe's — it took maybe a few pinch-fuls of chips before I started noticing that signature buildup up salty tang. Finally, rounding out my Trader Joe's experience was a potato flavor I found closer to that of a french fry than, say, a more vegetal baked potato. While the distinction was subtle, it was a quality I appreciated all the same. Had I compared Trader Joe's Sea Salt & Vinegar Chip and their Kettle Chips equivalent in a more casual setting, I likely would have found them difficult to distinguish from one another. With that said, I did pick up on a few subtle differences after a deep dive on both products. First off, while extra thickness is part of what sets Kettle Chips apart from regular potato chips , I thought my Trader Joe's chips were just the slightest bit thicker, whereas my name-brand Kettle Chips were a tad airier. That meant the former remained crunchy for a little longer, whereas my Kettle Chips' crunch wore off faster. Despite a famously bold, sometimes mouth-numbing flavor, salt and vinegar chips are surprisingly versatile. Starbucks salt and vinegar chips, for example, can be paired with coffee for a combo as satisfying as it is unconventional. In another instance of chain restaurant chip innovation, Red Lobster once added salt and vinegar chips to breaded shrimp . Simply put, there's something distinctly gratifying about a robust vinegary tang amplified by almost too much salt on crispy potato that has inspired these and other adventurous eats.

Kettle has arguably become one America's most beloved potato chip brands , producing what may well be the most iconic salt and vinegar chip available in grocery stores. Competing directly with Kettle Chips is Trader Joes, which sells Sea Salt & Vinegar Potato Chips with Avocado Oil. The Trader Joe's product even comes in a blue bag, reminiscent of the equivalent Kettle Chips packaging. I picked both brands' takes on the classic chip flavor from stores near my home in the suburbs of Las Vegas and tried them back-to-back. coreStoryFacts.text: The best chip is balanced: enough acidity to make your mouth pucker, plenty of salt, a strong potato flavor, and, most importantly, a chip sturdy enough to handle it all.I tried seven popular brands—Lay’s, Siete, Utz, Kettle Brand, Cape Cod, Deep River, and Pringles—to find the one that does salt and vinegar best.
Kettle BrandKettle Brand came extremely close to taking the top spot.

Deep RiverDeep River delivered the first truly satisfying vinegar punch of the group.The acidity hits immediately, but it comes across slightly sweeter and rounder than some of the sharper chips in this ranking.
The vinegar flavor is bright, acidic, and immediately satisfying, with enough salt to make the whole thing pop.My only complaint is how quickly the seasoning disappears.

The first few seconds of each bite are exactly what I want from salt and vinegar, but once that initial tang fades, you’re mostly left with a plain potato chip.Apparently that didn’t bother me too much, because I kept reaching back into the bag.

The flavor on the Kettle Cooked Olive Oil Potato Chips is a bit more subtle than some others, which I like, but it's the texture that gives them a slight edge over the ridge-style kettle chips in my book.
The chips are thin and crispy rather than hefty thanks to thinly sliced potatoes.
I compare them to the (upcoming) white truffle chips as far as texture, but the olive oil gives these chips a very different flavor.
When ranking chips, I knew which ones from Trader Joe's were already popular in my household, but I also tried some new flavor options to compare.
While there are tried-and-true crispy options, specialty selections like white truffle and Carolina Gold barbecue stand out from the pack.
There are also a few different texture varieties, including multiple ridge cut styles and even a super crispy lattice cut chip.
They're budget-friendly, too, so even when I'm looking for the best value, there are always a couple of options to add to my cart.
The crunchy texture is the best part of these chips, especially if you like a thinner chip like I do.
These are perfect for snacking — they aren't really heavy or dense but still give you a little something to enjoy.
The flavor isn't anything spectacular, but they have enough salt to satisfy a craving.
They're made out of thick slices of potatoes that are cut into ridges, cooked in sunflower oil, and finally sprinkled with sea salt.
The ingredients list is super short, perfect for those who are keeping a close eye on additives or preservatives.
Thanks to the addition of sea salt, these have the salty taste that you come to expect from a good potato chip without overpowering.
The heat doesn't come close to the ghost pepper and is more smoky than spicy, so don't worry about it being too overpowering.
If you're serving these to kids, their clothing and your upholstery have a better chance of coming out unscathed if you keep napkins nearby.
The salty flavor here goes with just about anything, even if you'll probably end up with broken chips in your bowl.
I like to add them as a crunchy topping on a sandwich, smash them to use as a salty breading for chicken, or pour them into a snack bowl.
Versatility is another thing that I appreciate in a potato chip, since I rarely get through a whole bag before they start to get stale.
You can use these chips in so many ways and never grow tired of their wonderful flavor.

extraction.body: Salt and vinegar chips, in my opinion, are one of the most divisive snacks out there. People either love that sharp, acidic punch or want absolutely nothing to do with it.I am firmly in the first camp, which is why I rounded up every bag I could find to see which brand makes the best ones. My ideal salt and vinegar chip is so aggressively vinegary that it practically makes my eyes water, but for this taste test, I tried to show a little restraint. The best chip is balanced: enough acidity to make your mouth pucker, plenty of salt, a strong potato flavor, and, most importantly, a chip sturdy enough to handle it all.I tried seven popular brands—Lay’s, Siete, Utz, Kettle Brand, Cape Cod, Deep River, and Pringles—to find the one that does salt and vinegar best. Instead of that clean, crisp crunch I want from a potato chip, these had an almost powdery quality that made each bite feel oddly dry. It built quickly into a harsh sourness that became almost nauseating after a few chips.Looking at the ingredient list, the seasoning relies on sodium diacetate along with several acids, and I could really taste that concentrated acidity. I love a powerful salt and vinegar chip, but this one crossed the line from punchy into overwhelming.6. PringlesPringles Salt Vinegar taste exactly like what you would expect: a familiar Pringles base with a tangy layer of vinegar seasoning.The flavor is pleasant, with a mild acidic bite and enough salt to make it clearly salt and vinegar. For this particular flavor, I want an actual potato chip with enough heft and crunch to stand up against all that acidity—not a potato-based crisp.If you already love Pringles, you’ll probably enjoy these. These have a great, substantial crunch, and the avocado oil imparts a mild flavor that lets the potato shine.What I didn't like was the serrano. The added pepper brings a mild vegetal heat that competes with the vinegar instead of letting it be the star. A noticeable salty tang still comes through, but I kept wishing I could taste more of it without the serrano getting in the way.Still, the crunch and vinegar were good enough to land these safely above the bottom two.4. Lay’sLay’s were a definite step up for me.The thin chip is light and crispy, and the potato itself tastes better than Utz. The seasoning has a clean, familiar salt and vinegar flavor with a pleasant sharpness that hits right away.I just wanted more of it.For a flavor this bold, Lay’s felt a little too polite. The vinegar fades quickly, leaving you mostly with the salty potato chip underneath. These are extremely easy to eat, but if I’m buying salt and vinegar chips, I want the vinegar to make itself known.3. Deep RiverDeep River delivered the first truly satisfying vinegar punch of the group.The acidity hits immediately, but it comes across slightly sweeter and rounder than some of the sharper chips in this ranking. That little touch of sweetness softens the sourness without eliminating it, and the seasoning lingers nicely after each bite.The kettle-cooked texture also gives these the sturdy crunch this flavor needs. They weren’t quite as balanced as my top two, but I appreciated that Deep River wasn’t afraid of vinegar.2. Kettle BrandKettle Brand came extremely close to taking the top spot. The chips have a fantastic crunch: thick and substantial without becoming painfully hard. The vinegar flavor is bright, acidic, and immediately satisfying, with enough salt to make the whole thing pop.My only complaint is how quickly the seasoning disappears. The first few seconds of each bite are exactly what I want from salt and vinegar, but once that initial tang fades, you’re mostly left with a plain potato chip.Apparently that didn’t bother me too much, because I kept reaching back into the bag. Cape CodCape Cod gave me the best overall combination of crunch, salt, potato, and vinegar.These have a bold kettle-cooked crunch that immediately makes them feel more substantial, followed by a vinegar flavor that is bright and tangy without becoming harsh. I could personally handle even more acidity, but the balance here is what ultimately earned them first place.The seasoning includes both white vinegar and apple cider vinegar, and I think that combination really sets these apart. The white vinegar gives you that clean acidic bite, while the apple cider vinegar adds a slightly fruitier, more rounded tang that gives the overall flavor more depth.Delish Test Kitchen Manager Alejandro Valdes Lora agreed, praising the great texture and fresh, crisp, slightly oily potato-chip flavor. He even went so far as to declare that Cape Cod “never disappoints.” I couldn’t agree more.After eating my way through seven bags, one thing became very clear: Kettle-cooked chips are the ideal vehicle for salt and vinegar. A flavor this strong needs a substantial potato chip underneath it. The thicker crunch gives all that sharp vinegar and salt something to push against, creating a much more satisfying bite.And while I will always support a chip acidic enough to make me tear up, Cape Cod proved that sometimes balance wins.

extraction.body: Trader Joe's is known for its delicious, unique-flavored snacks, and its potato chips are no exception. While there are tried-and-true crispy options, specialty selections like white truffle and Carolina Gold barbecue stand out from the pack. There are also a few different texture varieties, including multiple ridge cut styles and even a super crispy lattice cut chip. They're budget-friendly, too, so even when I'm looking for the best value, there are always a couple of options to add to my cart. My snack strategy includes a classic chip that I know I'll like, such as ridges or salty favorites, as well as a new flavor or texture variety to spice things up — and I wanted to know which ones should be added to my rotation. While I relied on potato chip-eating expertise carefully honed through years of backyard barbecues, picnics, and brown-bagging it for school lunch, a side-by-side taste test provided the best opportunity to really compare all the chip offerings Trader Joe's has on its shelves. I was happy to see plenty of options at my local TJ's, but you can also call ahead to reserve your favorites if you want something specific. One of the things I love most about shopping at Trader Joe's is popping in to pick up something I've never tried before, and the chip aisle is bursting with new options all the time. Without any further ado, let's get ranking. Unless you really love hot and spicy, the Ghost Pepper Potato Chips will probably be a bit too much to eat regularly. While ghost peppers aren't the hottest pepper in the world , they still pack quite a kick. The first couple of bites are pleasantly hot and tingly, but after a few chips, my mouth started burning. Unlike some flavored chips, these don't have a strong scent, distinct color, or messy exterior seasoning. So while you don't need to worry about getting a lot of residue on your fingers as you eat them, it does make it easy to reach for these by mistake and get more spice than you expected. In all, they're a fun variation on a standard potato chip, but not one that I'll be grabbing often. The lattice-style cut is one of the crispier options for Trader Joe's chips and my favorite part about this chip. They are sturdy enough to scoop up creamy homemade chip dips , which can also help tone down the heat. If I'm going to eat more than a few, I'll typically have some sour cream dip nearby, which pairs well with the spiciness here. The saddle potato chips come in a convenient tube that keeps their shape intact, which makes them a great option if you're packing snacks for a trip. But otherwise, these chips are only okay, especially when you compare them to other flavorful options on the same shelf. They're similar to other saddle-style chips in both texture and taste but only come in classic original rather than the huge variety of flavors that you find from other brands. If you like saddle chips, these are the only option from Trader Joe's, but they aren't on my list of favorite potato chips overall. The chips themselves have plenty of salt, but it's in the form larger seat salt crystals that aren't coated on or embedded into the chip. Because of this, it usually comes right off as you eat. The sea salt does add some extra crunch but it can be inconsistent from chip to chip. They are also a bit pricey for the size, costing around $2 for just over 5 ounces of chips. Most other bagged chips from Trader Joe's are around $3 and can be twice as big or more. But thanks to the sturdy packaging, at least you know that the chips won't get smashed and you'll get to enjoy the entire container without too many crumbs left at the bottom. If you like everything bagel seasoning, you'll love the Everything but the Bagel chips from Trader Joe's. It's made with a generous sprinkling of Everything but the Bagel, or E.B.T.B., seasoning . It became one of the "TJ's Hall of Fame" products almost as soon as it came out and the taste comes from salt, sesame seeds, poppy seeds, onion powder, garlic powder, and black pepper as well as a little bit of sugar and sesame oil to tie it all together. But if you have any reservations about the bold taste, start small when sampling these chips. They're bursting with flavor thanks to Trader Joe's signature seasoning blend, which Trader Joe's carries on other products, like crackers and cheese. If you like those, you'll love Everything but the Bagel chips as well. The chips have a nice crispy texture, likely thanks to the way that they are fried in small batches. Once they are cooled, the seasoning blend goes on in quite a large quantity, which is the main selling point for people who love these chips. It ultimately comes down to whether or not you like the E.B.T.B. seasoning, which is the dominant flavor of this chip. For me, it's solid, but not the best. Trader Joe's carries a few options in the ridge-cut style, each with a slightly different flavor. The salt and pepper chips are a bit denser than the other varieties from Trader Joe's, but it's the peppery flavor that sets it apart from the rest. The salt is a bit more subtle but still there, especially as you get toward the bottom of the bag. Don't confuse these with salt and vinegar chips, another popular flavor with chip-lovers, but one that Trader Joe's does not make. These have a peppery bite rather than a vinegar tang, but still boast a neutral chip taste that works with dips and salsas. If you want or need a gluten-free option, these have the iconic potato chip flavor and a nice crunch thanks to the ridges. They are particularly good for dipping because they are extra thick and sturdy. I scooped up heaps of sour cream and onion dip with these chips without breaking a single one. The salt and pepper flavor adds a little extra kick but isn't overpowering. Even my picky kids enjoyed this option. If you like a crispy chip that has less fat than a standard potato chip, the kettle-cooked chips are a fantastic choice. The crunchy texture is the best part of these chips, especially if you like a thinner chip like I do. These are perfect for snacking — they aren't really heavy or dense but still give you a little something to enjoy. They have 50% less fat and sodium than the Trader Joe's Ode to the Classic Potato Chips, which is the most similar in texture and taste. These are the least salty of the Trader Joe's chips in taste — something to keep in mind whether you're trying to lower your sodium intake or just want something simpler. extraction.body: Welcome to Dupe Detective, a column where I'll be reviewing a name brand food product's competitor product to find out how well it compares to, or even beats, the original. Despite a famously bold, sometimes mouth-numbing flavor, salt and vinegar chips are surprisingly versatile. Starbucks salt and vinegar chips, for example, can be paired with coffee for a combo as satisfying as it is unconventional. In another instance of chain restaurant chip innovation, Red Lobster once added salt and vinegar chips to breaded shrimp . Simply put, there's something distinctly gratifying about a robust vinegary tang amplified by almost too much salt on crispy potato that has inspired these and other adventurous eats. Kettle has arguably become one America's most beloved potato chip brands , producing what may well be the most iconic salt and vinegar chip available in grocery stores. Competing directly with Kettle Chips is Trader Joes, which sells Sea Salt & Vinegar Potato Chips with Avocado Oil. The Trader Joe's product even comes in a blue bag, reminiscent of the equivalent Kettle Chips packaging. I picked both brands' takes on the classic chip flavor from stores near my home in the suburbs of Las Vegas and tried them back-to-back. Ahead is a brief rundown of each item, before my thoughts on how Trader Joe's holds up against its name-brand competition. While the info isn't spotlighted on the front of the bag, Trader Joe's Sea Salt & Vinegar Potato Chips are, in fact, kettle-cooked. One of the foremost qualities that sets kettle-cooked chips apart from standard potato chips is their pronounced crunch, which is satisfying on its own, or even swapped into a nacho recipe for the crunchiest take on nachos possible. My Trader Joe's salt and vinegar chips were certainly crunchy, and I noticed they were the slightest bit thicker than the average potato chip too. In other words, I had nothing but positive thoughts about my Trader Joe's chips' texture. Foremost in my Trader Joe's Sea Salt & Vinegar Chips' flavor was malt vinegar. The fact I could taste that malty sweetness, more complex than a plain white vinegar, was a significant plus. Whereas some salt and vinegar chips are so bold they cause a tingling sensation from the get-go, I did notice a certain level of restraint from Trader Joe's — it took maybe a few pinch-fuls of chips before I started noticing that signature buildup up salty tang. Finally, rounding out my Trader Joe's experience was a potato flavor I found closer to that of a french fry than, say, a more vegetal baked potato. While the distinction was subtle, it was a quality I appreciated all the same. Had I compared Trader Joe's Sea Salt & Vinegar Chip and their Kettle Chips equivalent in a more casual setting, I likely would have found them difficult to distinguish from one another. With that said, I did pick up on a few subtle differences after a deep dive on both products. First off, while extra thickness is part of what sets Kettle Chips apart from regular potato chips , I thought my Trader Joe's chips were just the slightest bit thicker, whereas my name-brand Kettle Chips were a tad airier. That meant the former remained crunchy for a little longer, whereas my Kettle Chips' crunch wore off faster. In the flavor department, I found Kettle Chips' ratio of its two core ingredients slightly higher in salt — vinegar dominated the experience of my Trader Joe's chips, while the Kettle Chips formula featured salt and vinegar in roughly equivalent quantities. I also found Kettle Chips' vinegar flavor simpler, closer to a straight-up white vinegar. Plus, I picked up the slightest vegetal flavor from their potato component, contrasting with the more fried potato character of my Trader Joe's chips. Over time, I also noticed that the vinegar flavor had a tendency to fade, leaving a less complex salty potato aftertaste. There's no wrong choice between Trader Joe's Sea Salt & Vinegar Potato Chips and Seal Salt & Vinegar Kettle Chips — anyone craving a high-quality salt and vinegar chip would probably find both products satisfying. Nevertheless, true tingly chip-heads looking for the very best salt and vinegar chips on grocery store shelves should pick Trader Joe's over Kettle Chips. Previously, Trader Joe's Baked Cheese Crunchies beat Cheetos in a head-to-head , so for what it's worth, Trader Joe's remains a heavy hitter in the snack department. The qualities I preferred in my Trader Joe's salt and vinegar chips included their pronounced crunch, a more complex malt vinegar that lingered longer, and a fried potato flavor. For clarity's sake, those were all subtle elements that I was able to identify because my critical brain was actively looking for them, as opposed to glaring differences. That said, those differences were significant enough that, with both products in my pantry for a few days, I really only ever snacked on the Trader Joe's chips –leaving the slightly inferior Kettle Chips practically untouched. As much as both products are solid, then, it's fair to say that Trader Joe's makes the superior salt and vinegar chip. At my local Trader Joe's, in the Las Vegas-adjacent Henderson, Nevada, a 7-ounce bag of Sea Salt & Vinegar Potato Chips is $2.99. At an Albertsons between that Trader Joe's and my home, a 7.5-ounce bag of Seal Salt & Vinegar Kettle Chips is $4.29. Nutritionally, a 1-ounce serving of Trader Joe's salt and vinegar chips totals 140 calories, 7 grams of fat, 1 gram of which is saturated fat, 200 milligrams of sodium, 17 grams of carbs, 1 gram of fiber, and 2 grams of protein. An equivalent 1-ounce serving of salt and vinegar Kettle Chips equals 140 calories, 9 grams of fat, 1 gram of which is saturated fat, 180 milligrams of sodium, 15 grams of carbs, 2 grams of fiber, and 2 grams of protein. Altogether, then, the Trader Joe's chips are quite a bit cheaper but technically higher in sodium and carbs — those latter numbers, however, are minor enough to consider negligible. passages: Welcome to Dupe Detective, a column where I'll be reviewing a name brand food product's competitor product to find out how well it compares to, or even beats, the original.

Despite a famously bold, sometimes mouth-numbing flavor, salt and vinegar chips are surprisingly versatile. Starbucks salt and vinegar chips, for example, can be paired with coffee for a combo as satisfying as it is unconventional. In another instance of chain restaurant chip innovation, Red Lobster once added salt and vinegar chips to breaded shrimp . Simply put, there's something distinctly gratifying about a robust vinegary tang amplified by almost too much salt on crispy potato that has inspired these and other adventurous eats.

Kettle has arguably become one America's most beloved potato chip brands , producing what may well be the most iconic salt and vinegar chip available in grocery stores. Competing directly with Kettle Chips is Trader Joes, which sells Sea Salt & Vinegar Potato Chips with Avocado Oil. The Trader Joe's product even comes in a blue bag, reminiscent of the equivalent Kettle Chips packaging. I picked both brands' takes on the classic chip flavor from stores near my home in the suburbs of Las Vegas and tried them back-to-back. Ahead is a brief rundown of each item, before my thoughts on how Trader Joe's holds up against its name-brand competition.

While the info isn't spotlighted on the front of the bag, Trader Joe's Sea Salt & Vinegar Potato Chips are, in fact, kettle-cooked. One of the foremost qualities that sets kettle-cooked chips apart from standard potato chips is their pronounced crunch, which is satisfying on its own, or even swapped into a nacho recipe for the crunchiest take on nachos possible. My Trader Joe's salt and vinegar chips were certainly crunchy, and I noticed they were the slightest bit thicker than the average potato chip too. In other words, I had nothing but positive thoughts about my Trader Joe's chips' texture.

Foremost in my Trader Joe's Sea Salt & Vinegar Chips' flavor was malt vinegar. The fact I could taste that malty sweetness, more complex than a plain white vinegar, was a significant plus. Whereas some salt and vinegar chips are so bold they cause a tingling sensation from the get-go, I did notice a certain level of restraint from Trader Joe's — it took maybe a few pinch-fuls of chips before I started noticing that signature buildup up salty tang.

Finally, rounding out my Trader Joe's experience was a potato flavor I found closer to that of a french fry than, say, a more vegetal baked potato. While the distinction was subtle, it was a quality I appreciated all the same.

Had I compared Trader Joe's Sea Salt & Vinegar Chip and their Kettle Chips equivalent in a more casual setting, I likely would have found them difficult to distinguish from one another. With that said, I did pick up on a few subtle differences after a deep dive on both products. First off, while extra thickness is part of what sets Kettle Chips apart from regular potato chips , I thought my Trader Joe's chips were just the slightest bit thicker, whereas my name-brand Kettle Chips were a tad airier. That meant the former remained crunchy for a little longer, whereas my Kettle Chips' crunch wore off faster.

In the flavor department, I found Kettle Chips' ratio of its two core ingredients slightly higher in salt — vinegar dominated the experience of my Trader Joe's chips, while the Kettle Chips formula featured salt and vinegar in roughly equivalent quantities. I also found Kettle Chips' vinegar flavor simpler, closer to a straight-up white vinegar. Plus, I picked up the slightest vegetal flavor from their potato component, contrasting with the more fried potato character of my Trader Joe's chips. Over time, I also noticed that the vinegar flavor had a tendency to fade, leaving a less complex salty potato aftertaste.

There's no wrong choice between Trader Joe's Sea Salt & Vinegar Potato Chips and Seal Salt & Vinegar Kettle Chips — anyone craving a high-quality salt and vinegar chip would probably find both products satisfying. Nevertheless, true tingly chip-heads looking for the very best salt and vinegar chips on grocery store shelves should pick Trader Joe's over Kettle Chips. Previously, Trader Joe's Baked Cheese Crunchies beat Cheetos in a head-to-head , so for what it's worth, Trader Joe's remains a heavy hitter in the snack department.

The qualities I preferred in my Trader Joe's salt and vinegar chips included their pronounced crunch, a more complex malt vinegar that lingered longer, and a fried potato flavor. For clarity's sake, those were all subtle elements that I was able to identify because my critical brain was actively looking for them, as opposed to glaring differences. As much as both products are solid, then, it's fair to say that Trader Joe's makes the superior salt and vinegar chip.

extraction.body: The largest group of single-issue super PACs in United States history is pouring millions of dollars into congressional races across the country. Cryptocurrency groups outpaced online betting and data center development groups in federal corporate political spending this election cycle, according to Public Citizen . Crypto-tied organizations have contributed more than $200 million in this election cycle. The industry is hoping to repeat the success of 2024, when super PACs spent $250 million to elect pro-crypto lawmakers and reshape Congress. Crypto juggernaut Fairshake and its affiliated super PACs are throwing their support behind 33 House candidates — 19 Republicans and 14 Democrats — seen as key supporters of the industry's priorities. The network is prioritizing six House incumbents by injecting a baseline of $1 million into their campaigns. Republicans Bryan Steil of Wisconsin , who chairs a digital assets subcommittee in the lower chamber, as well as French Hill of Arkansas and Bill Huizenga of Michigan , who serve as the chair and vice chair of the House Financial Services Committee, respectively. Democratic lawmakers receiving at least $1 million from Fairshake include Reps. Janelle Bynum of Oregon; Derek Tran of California; and Steven Horsford of Nevada . Fairshake's spending spree has been supercharged by digital asset-focused companies, like cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase Global. Coinbase established itself as one of the largest corporate political donors in modern history in the 2024 election cycle, contributing $79 million to federal races, according to OpenSecrets . That included a $1 million dollar personal contribution from CEO Brian Armstrong to Fairshake in 2023. Coinbase donated $25 million to Fairshake's midterm efforts in 2025, according to the super PAC. "The ultimate goal is to make sure that we bring our 20th century financial system into the 21st century," Ryan VanGrack, vice chairman at Coinbase, told CNBC. "In an era where affordability is top of mind for American voters, it's important that we find a way that we can move money more cheaply, that we can invest more easily, and that we can transact more quickly, and fundamentally that is not something that Democrats or Republicans should oppose," he said. The industry faced pushback in the current Congress as it urged lawmakers to pass landmark crypto legislation. In September, the Clarity Act, a bipartisan set of market structure rules for digital assets, stalled in the Senate after Democrats argued it didn't do enough to prevent top government officials from profiting off crypto ventures. The stalemate over ethics comes as Americans grow increasingly gloomy toward government corruption. A Gallup poll released in September found a record 89% of U.S. adults say government corruption is widespread. Changing voter priorities also present a headwind for crypto's legislative efforts. The latest CNBC All-America Economic Survey this month found only 20% of respondents rate the economy as excellent or good, down from 27% in July. "Overwhelmingly, the issue right now is the affordability crisis," said Rep. Steven Horsford (D-Nev.), one of the three Democratic candidates Fairshake is giving more than $1 million. Horsford, who introduced bipartisan legislation in May to modernize federal tax laws for digital assets, said crypto is still on the minds of some voters, alongside economic uncertainty. "It definitely comes up in town halls and community meetings, in forums that I have, especially with small businesses who are looking to use digital assets and bitcoin," said Horsford. "They're being asked more and more by their consumers whether or not they take those those payments for services and goods." November's elections will test crypto's continued influence on Washington. The crypto industry is laser-focused on the Ohio Senate race between Democratic nominee, and former Senator, Sherrod Brown , a longtime crypto critic, and Republican Jon Husted, who is pro-crypto and currently holds the seat. Fairshake spent about $40 million to unseat Brown in 2024, when the then-Senate Banking Committee chairman had promoted tougher crypto regulation and stalled a House-passed market-structure bill. The super PAC this cycle told CNBC it has already spent $55 million to oppose Brown. A Marist poll conducted Oct. 15-18 showed Brown holding a four-point edge over Husted among likely voters statewide, within the margin of error of 4.5%. "A lot of these races are going to be extremely tight," said Mason Lynaugh, executive director of the advocacy group Stand With Crypto, launched by Coinbase in 2023. This election cycle, Stand With Crypto has endorsed a total of 45 candidates, 42 in the House of Representatives and three in the Senate. "We want to show that when we execute our program and we turn out those thousands or tens of thousands of Stand With Crypto advocates in these districts we are credibly ensuring that they get what they deserve for supporting crypto from the community that supports them," he added. Digital assets and infrastructure company Ripple spent a total of $63.65 million in federal contributions last election, according to OpenSecrets , and the company is spending millions again now. Ripple donated $25 million in 2025, according to Fairshake. Asked if the crypto industry got a good return on its investment, Stu Alderoty, Ripple's chief legal officer, told CNBC, "I think compared to where the industry was two years ago to where the industry is today, yes, I would say that that is a very good return." Alderoty pointed to the GENIUS Act, which established the first federal framework for dollar-pegged stablecoins. President Trump signed the bill into law in July 2025, the first-ever standalone crypto legislation in the United States. But the latest guidelines from these agencies aren't meant to replace legislation from Congress, and the window to pass new laws for crypto may be closing. Former New York governor Andrew Cuomo, now a board member of the crypto exchange OKX, told CNBC that lawmaking is unlikely if Congress changes hands in January. "You're going to have a Democratic Congress overseeing an administration, the Trump administration, where the regulators are making decisions under the scrutiny of a hostile Congress, and that is not a good place to be because the Congress will be at loggerheads with the administration," he said. Horsford, the Nevada congressman, told CNBC that time is of the essence. If the Clarity Act doesn't advance before the end of the year, Congress will have to start from scratch on a new market structure bill for digital assets. And crypto super PACs are hoping their spending still has the influence to shape which lawmakers work on the next round of legislation. "Regardless of who is elected in Congress, we're going to continue to see more regulatory clarity in this space," Coinbase's VanGrack, a former SEC senior advisor, told CNBC. "It may be an open question whether we get all the way across the goal line, but it's not an open question about whether we're going to have progress and continue to see progress in terms of regulatory clarity in crypto," VanGrack added. passages: Crypto groups have poured more than $200 million into the 2026 midterms, CNBC reported on October 31 , with the goal of pressuring Congress to write rules the industry can live with.
Voters pick a new Congress on Tuesday, November 3, and the question for anyone holding Bitcoin or building on-chain software is simple.
What do the midterm elections change for Bitcoin and the wider crypto market?
Industry money tops $200 million, the flagship bill failed 49 to 50 in September, and prediction markets favor a Democratic Congress that could slow legislation.
At the same time, Grayscale argues the long-run story rests on institutions and global adoption that no single vote can erase.
The honest answer starts with what has already happened.
That money flows mainly through Fairshake and its affiliated super PACs, along with the advocacy group Stand With Crypto.
The industry spent about $250 million in the 2024 elections, according to the same report, so this cycle’s total sits below that mark with polling day still ahead.
This analysis walks through the money, the races, the stalled legislation, the price action, and the scenarios that follow.
It separates reported facts from our own judgment, and it flags every place where the evidence runs thin.
Bitcoin Magazine cited concerns about AI sector valuations and higher oil prices, and it noted that the Federal Reserve held its October 27 and 28 meeting with the target range at 3.75% to 4%.
Our own coverage of that decision, Bitcoin at $80,100 as the Fed holds with two dissents seeking a hike , shows how much rate expectations already weigh on crypto before any election result arrives.
That view matters for Bitcoin traders, because a one-seat Senate margin decides committee chairs, floor schedules, and whether a 60-vote procedural threshold looks reachable.
The outlet put the October 2025 all-time high near $126,000 and described the current price as roughly 30% below year-ago levels.
By our math, $80,500 sits about 36% under that peak.
Other recaps this week showed Bitcoin dipping into the high $70,000s, so the range of recent prints runs from about $77,000 to $80,500.
Spending in House and Senate races is the pressure lever.
Campaign spending shows intent, not outcomes.
The $250 million spent in 2024 did not produce a finished market structure law by the end of 2025, and the 2026 push has run into a Senate wall.
Money opens doors, but it does not count votes.
Those same corporate donors face their own business pressure.
Coinbase’s latest quarter showed revenue falling 34% to $1.16 billion, as we detailed in our Coinbase Q3 2026 revenue report .
A clearer rulebook is a business goal as much as an ideological one.
The CLARITY Act is the bill that would have split oversight of digital assets between the SEC and the CFTC.
The House passed it on July 17, 2025, and a revised version cleared the Senate Banking Committee in May 2026.
A sharper way to use history is to ask what the market already knew.
Bitcoin dropped about 7% in October by one recap, before the vote, so some pre-election caution is likely priced in.
If results land close to prediction market odds, the surprise is small.
If they miss, price reacts to the gap, not the outcome itself.
It must be reintroduced in the next Congress.
Crypto groups want to look like a bipartisan constituency so that a change in control does not erase their standing.
Horsford told CNBC that the affordability crisis dominates voter concerns right now, and he also said time is of the essence on crypto legislation.
Those two statements pull in different directions.
A member can want crypto rules passed quickly and still admit that voters rank everyday costs far higher.
That would end Republican majorities in Congress at a moment when the crypto industry has leaned on a Republican-led push.
Macro factors such as Fed policy and AI valuation worries also weigh on Bitcoin right now.
For Bitcoin itself, the agency path matters less than for altcoins and token issuers, since Bitcoin already trades under a clearer commodity framing.
The sharper effect falls on newer tokens, staking products, and stablecoin businesses that need definitions to raise money and list on regulated venues.
Democratic senators who opposed the bill asked for tougher consumer protection and illicit finance rules, not for crypto to disappear.
CNBC reports that Fairshake set a $1 million baseline of support for six House incumbents.
Traders who cannot stomach a 10% swing should not carry that exposure through Tuesday night, and builders should plan for rules arriving from agencies instead of Congress.

coreStoryFacts.text: Cryptocurrency groups outpaced online betting and data center development groups in federal corporate political spending this election cycle, according to Public Citizen .
The industry is hoping to repeat the success of 2024, when super PACs spent $250 million to elect pro-crypto lawmakers and reshape Congress.
The super PAC this cycle told CNBC it has already spent $55 million to oppose Brown.
Former New York governor Andrew Cuomo, now a board member of the crypto exchange OKX, told CNBC that lawmaking is unlikely if Congress changes hands in January.
"Regardless of who is elected in Congress, we're going to continue to see more regulatory clarity in this space," Coinbase's VanGrack, a former SEC senior advisor, told CNBC.
The industry faced pushback in the current Congress as it urged lawmakers to pass landmark crypto legislation.

In September, the Clarity Act, a bipartisan set of market structure rules for digital assets, stalled in the Senate after Democrats argued it didn't do enough to prevent top government officials from profiting off crypto ventures.
But the latest guidelines from these agencies aren't meant to replace legislation from Congress, and the window to pass new laws for crypto may be closing.
And crypto super PACs are hoping their spending still has the influence to shape which lawmakers work on the next round of legislation.
"The ultimate goal is to make sure that we bring our 20th century financial system into the 21st century," Ryan VanGrack, vice chairman at Coinbase, told CNBC.

extraction.body: The largest group of single-issue super PACs in United States history is pouring millions of dollars into congressional races across the country. Cryptocurrency groups outpaced online betting and data center development groups in federal corporate political spending this election cycle, according to Public Citizen . Crypto-tied organizations have contributed more than $200 million in this election cycle. The industry is hoping to repeat the success of 2024, when super PACs spent $250 million to elect pro-crypto lawmakers and reshape Congress. Crypto juggernaut Fairshake and its affiliated super PACs are throwing their support behind 33 House candidates — 19 Republicans and 14 Democrats — seen as key supporters of the industry's priorities. The network is prioritizing six House incumbents by injecting a baseline of $1 million into their campaigns. Republicans Bryan Steil of Wisconsin , who chairs a digital assets subcommittee in the lower chamber, as well as French Hill of Arkansas and Bill Huizenga of Michigan , who serve as the chair and vice chair of the House Financial Services Committee, respectively. Democratic lawmakers receiving at least $1 million from Fairshake include Reps. Janelle Bynum of Oregon; Derek Tran of California; and Steven Horsford of Nevada . Fairshake's spending spree has been supercharged by digital asset-focused companies, like cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase Global. Coinbase established itself as one of the largest corporate political donors in modern history in the 2024 election cycle, contributing $79 million to federal races, according to OpenSecrets . That included a $1 million dollar personal contribution from CEO Brian Armstrong to Fairshake in 2023. Coinbase donated $25 million to Fairshake's midterm efforts in 2025, according to the super PAC. "The ultimate goal is to make sure that we bring our 20th century financial system into the 21st century," Ryan VanGrack, vice chairman at Coinbase, told CNBC. "In an era where affordability is top of mind for American voters, it's important that we find a way that we can move money more cheaply, that we can invest more easily, and that we can transact more quickly, and fundamentally that is not something that Democrats or Republicans should oppose," he said. The industry faced pushback in the current Congress as it urged lawmakers to pass landmark crypto legislation. In September, the Clarity Act, a bipartisan set of market structure rules for digital assets, stalled in the Senate after Democrats argued it didn't do enough to prevent top government officials from profiting off crypto ventures. The stalemate over ethics comes as Americans grow increasingly gloomy toward government corruption. A Gallup poll released in September found a record 89% of U.S. adults say government corruption is widespread. Changing voter priorities also present a headwind for crypto's legislative efforts. The latest CNBC All-America Economic Survey this month found only 20% of respondents rate the economy as excellent or good, down from 27% in July. "Overwhelmingly, the issue right now is the affordability crisis," said Rep. Steven Horsford (D-Nev.), one of the three Democratic candidates Fairshake is giving more than $1 million. Horsford, who introduced bipartisan legislation in May to modernize federal tax laws for digital assets, said crypto is still on the minds of some voters, alongside economic uncertainty. "It definitely comes up in town halls and community meetings, in forums that I have, especially with small businesses who are looking to use digital assets and bitcoin," said Horsford. "They're being asked more and more by their consumers whether or not they take those those payments for services and goods." November's elections will test crypto's continued influence on Washington. The crypto industry is laser-focused on the Ohio Senate race between Democratic nominee, and former Senator, Sherrod Brown , a longtime crypto critic, and Republican Jon Husted, who is pro-crypto and currently holds the seat. Fairshake spent about $40 million to unseat Brown in 2024, when the then-Senate Banking Committee chairman had promoted tougher crypto regulation and stalled a House-passed market-structure bill. The super PAC this cycle told CNBC it has already spent $55 million to oppose Brown. A Marist poll conducted Oct. 15-18 showed Brown holding a four-point edge over Husted among likely voters statewide, within the margin of error of 4.5%. "A lot of these races are going to be extremely tight," said Mason Lynaugh, executive director of the advocacy group Stand With Crypto, launched by Coinbase in 2023. This election cycle, Stand With Crypto has endorsed a total of 45 candidates, 42 in the House of Representatives and three in the Senate. "We want to show that when we execute our program and we turn out those thousands or tens of thousands of Stand With Crypto advocates in these districts we are credibly ensuring that they get what they deserve for supporting crypto from the community that supports them," he added. Digital assets and infrastructure company Ripple spent a total of $63.65 million in federal contributions last election, according to OpenSecrets , and the company is spending millions again now. Ripple donated $25 million in 2025, according to Fairshake. Asked if the crypto industry got a good return on its investment, Stu Alderoty, Ripple's chief legal officer, told CNBC, "I think compared to where the industry was two years ago to where the industry is today, yes, I would say that that is a very good return." Alderoty pointed to the GENIUS Act, which established the first federal framework for dollar-pegged stablecoins. President Trump signed the bill into law in July 2025, the first-ever standalone crypto legislation in the United States. But the latest guidelines from these agencies aren't meant to replace legislation from Congress, and the window to pass new laws for crypto may be closing. Former New York governor Andrew Cuomo, now a board member of the crypto exchange OKX, told CNBC that lawmaking is unlikely if Congress changes hands in January. "You're going to have a Democratic Congress overseeing an administration, the Trump administration, where the regulators are making decisions under the scrutiny of a hostile Congress, and that is not a good place to be because the Congress will be at loggerheads with the administration," he said. Horsford, the Nevada congressman, told CNBC that time is of the essence. If the Clarity Act doesn't advance before the end of the year, Congress will have to start from scratch on a new market structure bill for digital assets. And crypto super PACs are hoping their spending still has the influence to shape which lawmakers work on the next round of legislation. "Regardless of who is elected in Congress, we're going to continue to see more regulatory clarity in this space," Coinbase's VanGrack, a former SEC senior advisor, told CNBC. "It may be an open question whether we get all the way across the goal line, but it's not an open question about whether we're going to have progress and continue to see progress in terms of regulatory clarity in crypto," VanGrack added. This election cycle, Stand With Crypto has endorsed a total of 45 candidates, 42 in the House of Representatives and three in the Senate.

"We want to show that when we execute our program and we turn out those thousands or tens of thousands of Stand With Crypto advocates in these districts we are credibly ensuring that they get what they deserve for supporting crypto from the community that supports them," he added.

"It may be an open question whether we get all the way across the goal line, but it's not an open question about whether we're going to have progress and continue to see progress in terms of regulatory clarity in crypto," VanGrack added.

Voters pick a new Congress on Tuesday, November 3, and the question for anyone holding Bitcoin or building on-chain software is simple.
What do the midterm elections change for Bitcoin and the wider crypto market?
Industry money tops $200 million, the flagship bill failed 49 to 50 in September, and prediction markets favor a Democratic Congress that could slow legislation.
At the same time, Grayscale argues the long-run story rests on institutions and global adoption that no single vote can erase.
The honest answer starts with what has already happened.
That money flows mainly through Fairshake and its affiliated super PACs, along with the advocacy group Stand With Crypto.
The industry spent about $250 million in the 2024 elections, according to the same report, so this cycle’s total sits below that mark with polling day still ahead.
This analysis walks through the money, the races, the stalled legislation, the price action, and the scenarios that follow.
It separates reported facts from our own judgment, and it flags every place where the evidence runs thin.
Bitcoin Magazine cited concerns about AI sector valuations and higher oil prices, and it noted that the Federal Reserve held its October 27 and 28 meeting with the target range at 3.75% to 4%.
Our own coverage of that decision, Bitcoin at $80,100 as the Fed holds with two dissents seeking a hike , shows how much rate expectations already weigh on crypto before any election result arrives.
That view matters for Bitcoin traders, because a one-seat Senate margin decides committee chairs, floor schedules, and whether a 60-vote procedural threshold looks reachable.
The outlet put the October 2025 all-time high near $126,000 and described the current price as roughly 30% below year-ago levels.
By our math, $80,500 sits about 36% under that peak.
Other recaps this week showed Bitcoin dipping into the high $70,000s, so the range of recent prints runs from about $77,000 to $80,500.
Spending in House and Senate races is the pressure lever.
Campaign spending shows intent, not outcomes.
The $250 million spent in 2024 did not produce a finished market structure law by the end of 2025, and the 2026 push has run into a Senate wall.
Money opens doors, but it does not count votes.
Those same corporate donors face their own business pressure.
Coinbase’s latest quarter showed revenue falling 34% to $1.16 billion, as we detailed in our Coinbase Q3 2026 revenue report .
A clearer rulebook is a business goal as much as an ideological one.
The CLARITY Act is the bill that would have split oversight of digital assets between the SEC and the CFTC.
The House passed it on July 17, 2025, and a revised version cleared the Senate Banking Committee in May 2026.
A sharper way to use history is to ask what the market already knew.
Bitcoin dropped about 7% in October by one recap, before the vote, so some pre-election caution is likely priced in.
If results land close to prediction market odds, the surprise is small.
If they miss, price reacts to the gap, not the outcome itself.
It must be reintroduced in the next Congress.
Crypto groups want to look like a bipartisan constituency so that a change in control does not erase their standing.
Horsford told CNBC that the affordability crisis dominates voter concerns right now, and he also said time is of the essence on crypto legislation.
Those two statements pull in different directions.
A member can want crypto rules passed quickly and still admit that voters rank everyday costs far higher.
That would end Republican majorities in Congress at a moment when the crypto industry has leaned on a Republican-led push.
Macro factors such as Fed policy and AI valuation worries also weigh on Bitcoin right now.
For Bitcoin itself, the agency path matters less than for altcoins and token issuers, since Bitcoin already trades under a clearer commodity framing.
The sharper effect falls on newer tokens, staking products, and stablecoin businesses that need definitions to raise money and list on regulated venues.
Democratic senators who opposed the bill asked for tougher consumer protection and illicit finance rules, not for crypto to disappear.
CNBC reports that Fairshake set a $1 million baseline of support for six House incumbents.
Traders who cannot stomach a 10% swing should not carry that exposure through Tuesday night, and builders should plan for rules arriving from agencies instead of Congress.

There were also instances of students running through the crowd, which may have contributed to reports of a larger disturbance. More than 3,000 people attended the game, making it one of the district’s most highly attended events. To help manage crowd size and maintain safety, MSCS is implementing a cap on ticket sales and reviewing additional safety measures for future sporting events.

Memphis-Shelby County Schools (MSCS) is considering additional security measures at future sporting events after multiple fights broke out during Friday night's football game between Southwind and Germantown.
In a statement provided to FOX13, MSCS confirmed that the district was aware of reports of a large fight at the Oct. 30 game.
However, they said the district's review indicated there were several separate altercations rather than one large fight.
According to the district, MSCS security officers and Shelby County sheriff's deputies responded to the disturbances and quickly broke up the fights.
The individuals involved were subsequently escorted out of the stadium.
District officials also reported instances of students running through the crowd, which may have contributed to reports of a larger disturbance.
The incidents occurred during one of the district's most heavily attended sporting events.
Following the disturbances, district officials are evaluating potential changes to security procedures and crowd management at future sporting events.
Among the measures under consideration are limiting ticket sales, increasing security personnel at games and exploring additional options to better manage large crowds.
The district has not announced whether any of the proposed measures will be implemented or when changes could take effect.
MSCS did not provide information about possible injuries, arrests or disciplinary actions in its statement.
FOX13 will continue following developments as the district evaluates its security procedures for future sporting events.
FULL STATEMENT FROM MEMPHIS-SHELBY COUNTY SCHOOLS:

"We’re aware of reports about a large fight at Friday night’s Southwind–Germantown game. Our review indicates there were four to five separate physical altercations. MSCS security officers and sheriff’s deputies broke them up promptly, and the individuals involved were escorted out of the stadium. There were also instances of students running through the crowd, which may have contributed to reports of a larger disturbance."

"More than 3,000 people attended the game, making it one of the district’s most highly attended events. MSCS is exploring additional safety measures for future sporting events, including capping ticket sales, increasing security at games and other options to help manage crowds and support safety."

extraction.body: For generations, most Americans have deposited their money in banks knowing that if somehow things went sideways, their funds would be covered by the full force of the government's treasury. Up to $250,000 in losses are covered through the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), born out of the ashes of the Great Depression. Crypto investors are probably wishing for an FDIC equivalent after Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, was hacked on Oct. 29, with an estimated impact of $6.3 billion, raising questions about the recovery of stolen funds and the broader fallout for crypto markets. About $3 billion of the stolen assets has been frozen so far, according to a Binance security update. In a security update on Saturday, the exchange said it had replenished 90% of stolen assets and was committed to covering the remaining 10%. Blockchain investigators at TRM Labs and Chainalysis have linked the attack to North Korea , but neither the U.S. government or Binance has publicly confirmed any source for the hack. Understanding how crypto is protected online and what mechanisms exist to serve a role similar to insurance is increasingly important as more Americans invest in cryptocurrency. Roughly one in five U.S. adults say they have invested in, traded, or used crypto , according to Pew Research Center, a figure that is even higher among upper income households (27%). The Securities and Exchange Commission's research from 2024 and 2025 puts that figure closer to 15%, and estimated that roughly 9% of the investing public owned crypto at the time of its survey. Its survey work indicates cryptocurrency ownership is more common for younger individuals, men, and those with higher risk tolerance, but also possessing higher financial literacy. While Binance was making good on its pledge in the aftermath of the hack to cover all losses with its SAFU (Secure Asset Fund for Users) and other company's funds — and that there's no evidence of a wallet private-key leak in this incident — Nikolas Behar, a cybersecurity expert and professor at the University of San Diego, said crypto investors need to understand when using crypto platforms that a pledge is just a pledge "until there's an actual payout." If something happens to your crypto, most consumers are left to navigate a patchwork of options that vary from exchange to exchange and are often very ambiguous. Many exchanges say customers will be paid back if something goes wrong. Josephine Wolff, professor of cybersecurity policy at The Fletcher School at Tufts University, said there "really aren't any legal protections for crypto assets equivalent to FDIC insurance." Customers could try to sue a hacked exchange, she said, for instance by claiming it was negligent, or may recover some funds if the exchange declares bankruptcy, as happened with FTX. But "there's no guarantee of compensation," she said. Michael Tanguma, co-founder and CEO of Onramp Bitcoin, a bitcoin financial services and custody firm, said that when an exchange is hacked, customers are usually repaid, "but only because the exchange decides to pay and has the money to do so." "Nothing in the law requires it to," Tanguma said. "Some stolen funds can be frozen. Tether and Circle, the companies behind the two largest dollar-backed tokens, froze billions of dollars of this week's stolen money, and law enforcement occasionally recovers assets years later," Tanguma said. But he added that bitcoin has no company behind it that can freeze it, so once it leaves your control, it is almost always gone. Customers who lose funds individually are in a very different situation than those caught up in an exchange attack. "When your own account is compromised, through a stolen password, a phishing link, or a hijacked phone number, the outlook is much worse," Tanguma said, noting that exchanges generally treat those losses as the customer's problem, and because crypto transactions are final once confirmed, there is no bank to call and no charge to dispute. Tanguma said keeping coins offline can protect against the kind of attack that hit Binance, though there are other risks associated with this digital security approach. "The stolen funds came from wallets the exchange keeps connected to the internet to process everyday withdrawals, not from its offline reserves," Tanguma said. But he added that the details of this hack point to a larger problem. "Binance says no keys were leaked. The attackers manipulated the system that approves withdrawals, the same approach used in last year's $1.5 billion theft from Bybit, which targeted a transfer out of cold storage," Tanguma said, noting that every custody setup has a weak point, and in most of them it is a single one. "On an exchange, that point is the company: its employees, its approval systems, its finances, and its willingness to repay you," Tanguma said. When you hold your own coins, he said, that point is you: a lost device, a backup found by the wrong person, a tampered device bought from an unofficial seller, a transaction approved under pressure, or a family unable to reach the funds after a death. "Moving savings off an exchange trades one kind of risk for another. It does not remove risk," Tanguma said. Sarah Downey, executive vice president and global blockchain and digital assets advisory leader at Lockton, an insurance brokerage, said other factors also come into play in determining whether you can get your crypto back, including how quickly the theft is discovered, where the funds were moved, whether the exchange or wallet provider has insurance that covers the event, and whether it holds enough reserves to repay customers. "Some companies have set up FDIC-like insurance or other backstops, but whether these pay out depends heavily on the facts of each case. Even without insurance, many exchanges try to repay customers from their own reserves to protect both their customers and their own reputation," Downey said. Crypto exchange reimbursements have followed other security compromises, such as after rogue overseas support agents were bribed to help scam Coinbase customers in May 2025. Bitget, another major exchange, had to tap an in-house fund to reimburse customers after a $388 million hack in September. Bitget CEO Gracy Chen said its User Protection Fund, which held more than $464 million, covered the loss. "The Protection Fund was created for moments like this and absorbed the financial impact of the incident," Chen said in a post on X at the time. By comparison, Binance's emergency reserve, the Secure Asset Fund for Users, or SAFU, is estimated at roughly $1 billion to $1.2 billion, and excluding the funds that were frozen, this represented about one-third of the loss. The company said it had set aside more than $6.34 billion in company funds and already held more than $5 billion in corresponding token assets. Downey said the steps to take if your crypto is hacked depend on whether investors self-custody or use a third party, such as a regulated exchange. "If they use a third party, they should check that most funds are stored offline or protected with multi-party computation. An investor's own funds should also be stored separately from the exchange's own funds," Downey said, adding that customers should also understand how the custodian authorizes transactions and governs storage. Ryan Reck, founder and principal of Reck Advisory, an independent cybersecurity advisory firm, points to the lack of oversight of crypto. "Crypto has no undo button. Once a transfer confirms, there's no chargeback and no one who can reverse it," Reck said. In some cases, stolen funds can be frozen by an exchange that receives them, or by a stablecoin issuer at a specific blockchain address, but tracing the money and getting it back are two different things. Among the common reasons investors cite for making crypto investments is diversification away from traditional assets, as well as use of crypto as a digital version of gold, investing in the decentralization of finance theme, and betting that as more institutions adopt digital currencies, that will serve as a tailwind. And there's of course also speculation. Today, there are ways to invest in crypto that don't require holding the underlying currency in a wallet, such as exchange-traded funds, including the iShares Bitcoin Trust ( IBIT ), which has over $62 billion in assets, or the Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund ( FBTC ), which has over $15 billion in assets. There are also diversified crypto index ETFs holding a basket of top digital currencies, including the Bitwise 10 Crypto Index Fund ( BITW ) and the Grayscale CoinDesk Crypto 5 ETF ( GLDC ). For investors who want to hold crypto directly, Reck says that before trusting any platform, ask four questions:
